THE SHIP'S COMPANY. She's the captain of the Waterwitch, And a very good captain too, Anl she's trim,and neat from her hat to her feet, And her eyes are blue—true blue. „,_ And whenever we meet upon the shore Or sailing across the bay, • I cry,. "goat ahoy 1" like a true sailor And this is what I say: "Oh, make me your boa's'n or your mate," say "And let me sail with you, For you are the captain of the Waterwitch, And a very good captain too." Then she lifts her eyes with sweet surprise: "The mate, that sails with me, Must honour and obey, and never say me nay, On land or on the sea." "Then I'll be your mate, sweetheart," say I • (And she gives me her pretty hand), 'For I want no more on land or shore Than to live at your command." . So I beg to state, she's made me mate, And together we sail the blue, For she is the captain of the Waterwitch, And I—am all the crew. • FREDERIC E. He can go to the circus in the afternoon and evening without paying a farthing, also to inqueats' and hangings. He has free tickets to the theatres, gets wedding cake sent to him and some- times gets licked, but not often, for he can pay things back in the next issne, which he generally does. While other folks have to go to bed early, be can sit up every night and see all that is going on. How roomer WAS TAUGHT TO PLAY THE CRITIC.— Everyone knows that Germans are fond of music. A - certain gentleman who lived in Darmstadt some fifty years ago was so fond of it that he was not happy till every member of his household could play or sing some- thing. Each of them learnt to take part in his concerts in time—eech, at least, but the dog'; and what could he do, poor fellow? He might, indeed, wag his tail and bark; but it was generally at the wrong place, until his master made up his mind that Poodle must lesen some how to be musical. Accordingly Mr. S— took care that the dog should be in the room when the practices or concerts were going on, and should stand quite close to him. As he himself conducted, or beat time, he had a little cane in his hand, and whenever someone played or sang a wrong note, down came his master's cane on the dog's back. . Although he was not much hurt, of eourse Poodle objected to this treatment, and used to howl and growl. By-and-by the dog was c'ever enough to understand that there had been a mistake by seeing his master just shake the stick at him, and at last a mere look waelenough to make him howl most horribly. So, gradually the spaniel of Darmstadt—for it was a spaniel, although its name was Poodle—became a real mu cal c itic. It went with its master to all concerts and operas, and woe bAide the poor performer who made a mistake! Up went the dog's ears, his teeth were shown RS if he were going to bite everyone, and he howled until his master signalled to him to leave off.— Little Folks for October. WHAT'S IN A NAME ?—The pronunciation of English surnames, as sometimes indicated by rhymes and quibbles. is a matter; of old literary history. A few notable instances are set forth in the following little paper, but no pretence is made to exhaust a theme so fertile and so attractive. Explaining the relationship of the Duke of Wellington to the family that had pro- duced the famous preachers. John and Charles Wesley, De Quincey has indicated that the theory of expansion from the name Wesley into Wellesley is an entire mis- take, for that the process of chump has been just the • other way. The two families, in fact, had been originally one; founded—so says De Quincey—on a connection with Wells Cathedral. The contraction of Wellesley into Wes'ey was due, no doubt, to household usage, the change obeying a common law of nominative mutations. Selinger was the pronounciat ion of St. Leger as long back as Elizabeth, and indeed longer, seeing that a favourite Court dance in the time of Henry VIII. was called Sel- inger's Round. Pope gives us the key to pronouncing St. John, where in apostrophising Bolingbroke, he compels the reader to follow the fashion et iit dar, and give the line as if it were 'written, Arise, my Sinjen." Of the same order of surnames is St. Maur, which has long Since settled, as regards one distinguished branch of the family, into Seymour. Cavendish—the name of the illustrious family of Earls and Dukes of Devon, as of anteir celebrated predecessors in fame, Sir William, their ite464414r, aßther Of the "Life of Wo'sey," and eir ; •#or, who sailed round the WC.'ld, and Thomas, tne navig.a. "en hie second voyage in died off the coast of Braze —was for some centuries pronounce... the z. in Menzies, and laying the stress u on tile gol the first syllable, it has teen usual to sound that name Monies. Marjoribanks and Cholmondeley, as is av, ll- known, are corrupttd into Marehhartes and Chumley. For the true guttural pronunciation of Buchanan, the nearest approach to which, perhaps, by a Sothron is Bouhanan, no apology is. necessary. Another Gaelic name, also given with a guttural sound, is Reach. Angus Reach, a Celt of the true type, well known in light literature:by Londoners some 30 years ago, was t e sub- ject of a playful little story to :hi effect that he Was thus addressed by Thackeray at tho dinner-table : " Mr. Re-ach, you take a pe-ach 2" Peeps, or as some have it, Pips, is the pronunciation of Pepys anl so it was, there is good reason ler believing, when the artless diarist was the Secretary of the Admiralty be- tween 1660 and 1688. As Peeps makes Peeps or Pips when spoken, so does Welnyte maize Weems or Wims. It has been:customary, and tee practice obtains with many persons, even at the prose t day, if, indeei, it be not right, to call Leveson-Ciower, Lewson-Gore.—Casseli's Saturday Journal. I mentioned recently that the Czar has sent a troika to the German Emperor, together with three Russian horses to draw it, and a native coachman to drive them. Considerable sensation has been caused in Berlin owing to the publication of a state- ment that this man is the man who drove the late Czar on the day of his assassination.

The result of Mr. Jackson's flying tour through Ireland as seen in Sir M. Hicksbeach's speech on Tuesday. "If help was to be given, the question arose how it might best be given. It might be given, fortunately, in many places by the construction ot railways under the Act of 1889." Good God! One would think that a starving peasantry could be fed on fish-plates and sleepers!

The Salvationists are treating the death of Mrs. Booth in characteristic fashion. The " War Cry" appears without any mourning reorder, and fronts an article signed " Your affectionate General," and entitled "Home at Last," with the huge cross-head- ing "Mrs. Booth's Promotion to Glory." The Sal- vationists obviously do not believe with most Christians in the exceeding mournfulness of death.

Brave Colonel Caddell gives Mr. Morley the lie direct. Good. We would not wish the issue raised more fairly and squarely. It is the word of an English statesman of thehighest reputation—an ex- Chief Secretary to boot--who goes over to Tipperary to test the official reports by the evidence of his own eyes, against the word of a police officer. Which will the English public accept? We prefer Mr. Morley. Mr. Balfour and his friends are welcome the policeman.

A fact which has often puzzled me in connection with the Queen's attire was explained to me on Saturday in a talk with .a clever man dressmaker in Bond-street, who has frequently made for Royalty. Ile assaures me that the Queen does not always wear the same dress, as I imagined, but that she has them made a dozen at a time, all after the same pattern. They measure 36in. in front. 1 was shown one of the black silk skirts, and was amused at the large flat pocket placed on the outside.

A legal contemporary, who has been looking the matter up, has discovered that the re-consecration of St. Paul's will probably not be rendered neces- sary by the suicide on Sunday last. "Reconcilia- tion " is said to be all that is required. This is very satisfactory. But we should like fuller narti- culars as to who it is that is to be reconciled, and to what, as well as how. If we might make a sug- gestion, the occasion seems to demand something between an auto-da-fe and a housewarming,

Here is a little item of news that will interest the Church and Stage Guild. During J. L. Toole's re- cent season in Brisbane, the capital of Queensland, his leading lady, Miss Irene Vanbrugh, was enter- tained at the episcopal palace by the Anglican Bishop, Dr. Thornhill Webber, late rector of St. John the Evangelist, Holborn. Miss Vanbrugh is under- stood to be a daughter of a canon a the Church of England, and, es all patrons of Toole's Theatre are aware, is a clever, cultured, and well-favored young lady.

By the way, Lady Colin Campell has been spend ing some time at Boulogne this year, where she dis- tinguished herself by her bold swimming. She insisted on swimming out until she was recalled by a vigorous blowing of horns, the irritating, idiotic custom by which the authorities at French bathing places debar good swimmers from showing their powers. By the way, another conspicuous visitor at Boulogne was Dr. Tanner, who lost his money with cheerful regularity at " chemin de far" at the Casino, and waltzed with genial forgetfulness of politics with the wife of a Tory

Miss Edith J. Bain, the young lady journalist who- made herself famous by endeavouring to obtain admission to the Reporters' Gallery at tho House of Commons while representing the-" Woman's Penny Paper," is about to sever her connection with that paper, having accepted an engagement on Michael Davitt's newspaper, the "Labour World." Miss Bain is well-known in other circles than the news- paper world, as she has been entering with much energy into the question of woman's work in fac- tories and the formation of trade unions for the women of the East-end; and she can speak on the platform as well as she can write.

Mr. Sheriff Jinni's bon mot at the Sheriffs' breakfast deserves a permanent place in the civic annals. In eloquently describing the manifold virtues of hie successors, he observed dryly that "one of the in- coming sheriffs had come to them from across the ocean, while the other bad been found on the Strand !" The roar of langhter which rose from the "cantors' table" might have been heard half a mile off, and the junior sheriff expressed his fears that he should not hear the last of the joke till his dying day. The cheering match kept up between the friends of the two sheriffswas more enthusiastic than dignified.

I have just heard of a notable'precedure adopted by a surgeon for the relief of a patient. A man came for advice concerning his forearm, which had been broken some months previously. Despite the most careful treatment there had been no union of the bones. The arm was perfectly useless and the muscles all wasted. The surgeon freshened the fractured ends of the bones and inserted between the ends nine small pieces of the thigh bone of a rabbit, killed for the purpose. The case did well. In about four months afterwards, perfect union had occurred between the respective bone, and shortly afterwards the man was able to resume his employ- ment as a tram conductor.

A learned ecclesiologist, the late Rev. T. W. Moss- man, gave the devotion of a life-time to investiga- ting the constitution and customs of the early Church. I believe the conclusion at which he arrived was that the primitive bishops were women. This discovery was his magnum opus. Content with this, he lived and died a happy, though an unre- warded man. Something of the same kind seems to have been revealed to the editor of the " Pall Mall Gazette," who, apropos of Mrs. Booth's death, writes of "the woman as bishop." "The bishop as woman" wonld be a more intelligible conception; and if the epithet old were added, the application would in certain dioceses be even more distinct.

Miss Helen Gladstone is sketched with a free hand by an American lady who has been staying at Newnh am College, Cambridge:—" Miss Gladstone is exceedingly original person. In looks she A.- • her father, and she has, I fancy his " ni,-7.1 laughing, joking, telling I . , rveisteamlitbyle. Sh e , stories. She keeps the ci igli table ,fl a roar, 1.7.0 eed whenever I hear a commotion, I turn to eee if Miss Gladstone is not about, and she generally is. She is utterly regardless of dress ; comes down to seven o'clock dinner in a gingham, and for lunch and garden parties gets herself up to look like the strong-minded practical wife of a country minister: She seems frank, sympathetic, kindly, and has great magnetism. Streams of power flow out of her eyes. It amuses one to think what a shock she would be to many Boston people."

The police are now said to have changed their tactics, if they can be said to have ever had any tactics, in the search after " Jack the Ripper.' Their old plan was to keep the women off the streets. Now they encourage them to go where they please, and practically employ them as detectives,promising to keep them in view and provide speedy help in case of an attack. Perhaps the most significant part of the whole business is that the women are perfectly willing to fall in with this line of tactics. "I have only to die once," said one of them," and I'd not mind being murdered by Jack the Ripper,' if it led to the brute being caught. The people speak, so kind and sympathisin', too, about the women he has killed, that I'd not object to being ripped up by him to be talked about so nice after I'm dead. And better sudden death than slow star- vation." This is what life in the East-end is coming to mean to some thousands of creatures in the year of grace ISOO.

• The proposal to tax bachelors for being bachelors is never likely to become law. But if this were so, it is dear that those men whom no one will marry ought not to have to pay for want of appreciation of the other sex. Any bachelor, who could show that he has proposed and been refused, ought to be exempted from the tax, which should, on the other hand, be levied on any spinster who can be shown to have refused an offer of marriage.

What next? A tradesman at Enfield drives out his wife and child in his trade cart, and is fined ss. and costs for keeping his "carriage " without a license. To make things worse the man was not even taking the " missus " out for a drive. He was going 0 market, and his wife went with him to mind the pony in his absence—in other words, she was assisting the husband in his business. If that is contrary to law—and the magistrate says there is no doubt it is—what about all the cartloads that drive out of town on a Sunday afternoon?

The Rev. Henry White, who died on Tuesday, if not one of the ablest, was at least one of the best known clergymen in London. He had a host of per- sonal friends among all classes. As Chaplain of the 1-iouse of Commons, he was on the best terms with members of all shades of opinion. As Chaplain of the Royal Chapel of the Savoy, he welcomed mem- bers of the cloth of whatever colour—High, Low, or Broad—from America and the Colonies to his pulpit. Ile was well-known, and had many friends in theatrical and Bohemian circles, and has married more actors and actresses than any pastor in Lon- don.

An excellent story reaches me from a certain watering-place on the east coast, where one of the local lodging-house keepers runs a tin tabernacle on the convenient principle of "sea air, a Christian welcome, and two guineas a Sunday." A few Sun- days ago, in consequence of the wet, the congrega- tion was abnormally small, and the deacons deliber- ately docked half the fee due to a youthful preacher who had been engaged to officiate. Early in the following week one of the best known and most eloquent Nonconformist divines in London put in an appearance, and wad at once bombarded by the wily chapel proprietor, who saw in him a certain " draw " for a sermon on the succeeding Sunday. Dr. Blank, however, soon heard of the treatment to which his humble colleague in the ministry had been subjected, and he sternly insisted on a fee of five guineas. This demand was after some demur agreed to, and when the day came the chapel was packed from floor to ceiling. The joy of the astute trader in theology was short-lived, for the doctor sternly declined to enter the pulpit until the guinea, unlawfully stopped on the previous Sunday was promptly paid up. This was done, and next morn- ing the popular orator, whose discourse gave uni- versal satisfaction, divided his earnings between a local charity and the young man, and what was worse, made no secret of having done so.

literature, and for holding sPrvice, and into one of the latter I found my way. singing is an import- ant feature in all these services and is most heartily taken up by the whole congregation. A little mat- ter follows, between the singing and the discourse, which is not quite so heartily taken up, judging by the amount of forcible language used to introduce it. The collection is always an interesting feature to church-goers, but I never saw, or heard, such downright cheek, excuse the term, as was here ex- hibited, although I am told by some .of my folk it is a 'regular thing. "Now my friends," said the beggar in chief. "we want a hundred dollars this afternoon. We want about two of you to put in twenty-five dollars each and the rest can give quart- ers and nickels. I always notice when the colleo- tion is going on that some of you cannot find your purses, some are busy talking to their neighbours and don't see the hat, and others are looking round for the clock just when the hat reaches them. This won't do, attend to the collection because we must have money." I thought this pretty tall talk, so tall in fact that it proved beyond my reach, I managed to have a good time amongst them and lots of dis- cussion and came away thinking of the Ranters and Jumpers of thirty years ago. Hearing that the Spiritualists were holding a Convention in Fruit Vale on the Sunday morning, I went there. The spirits are, like the monks of old, good judges as to desirable locations. I found them fixed in a most splendid grove of eucalyptus trees, the perfume from which was enough to:tempt even the angels, who were encouraged to put in an appearance by large posters on which appeared in large. characters 41

" WELCOME To-TITE ANGELS-! I fancied at first there was something personal about these posters, and that the spirits must have warned them that I was coming; perhaps I was mistaken. However that may be, I had not been on the ground many minutes before one of them—l mean a spiritualist, not an angel—told me that a w3man was following me. I asked him what she wanted. " he answered, "you will be sorry if you don't take notice of her." This was a fine predicament, as I had already one lady on hand, and one who claimed to be noticed. The other " wasn't material," SO I left her in the "shade." I walked about considerably, looking for the shadowy visitors, but left in a rather sceptical state of mind as to their having put in an appearance. All this gadding about suited me famously. I got plenty of fresh, warm, air, saw a bit of the country, and became convinced that of all people who on earth do dwell, none like to be gulled like the 'cute American. From the country lanes I betook myself to the shores of the Pacific, and spent a day watch- ing the women and children paddling. Lying on my back listening to the tremendous rollers as they broke on the shore, I thought of Blackpool and Southport, and of the happy hours I had spent at New Brighton. But this sort of thing don't last for ever, and I had to hie me back to the city sand- hills, with their fleas ever ready to welcome good pure blood well charged with ozone.

In my last letter to, the •` Examiner," I promised to say a few words on sehools and schooling. Since this promise was made,. I have been, undergoing some very unpleasant sensations. Rheumatic fever, and muscular rheumatism as a sedative, are net very encouraging preliminaries to educational essay writing, so I beg to put the matter on on side until health and strength are- better than at present. Yes„ I have had at least two months of a vacation in which to study the ups and down of poor human nature_ There is no fear of me having to say with one of Gilbert's heroes,

Oh, don't the days seem, sad and long When all goes right and nothing wrong; And isn't life exceeding_flat When there's nothingat all to grumble at ! The days were indeed sad, and long, especially the nights, and when one's joints, .fingers and toes .are swollen to something like double their normal size it must be allowed there is something to grumble at, Still when all the pain is gone, and only to be remembered as a disagreeable interlude in life's tragical farce, there is something,especially nice in listening to, and following out the doctor's parting words—" Well, I have done all i can for you now, and all that you want is plenty of good food and fresh air." I managed to get the former, for bad as things have been at times we have never gone short of good food, and for the latter I determined to take short jaunts outside and AWL FROM TDB CITY'S MADDING CROWD.. San Francisco has a location which is peculiar. Placed on a long sandy peninsular, and with un- dulations, which, if allowed to go on, would have approached the mountains, pedestrian exercises tend to severe dimensions. There is,.certainly, the cable 'car system which is an agreeable method of trans- portation and much more acceptable to stiff joints. Out, and away from the city one is bound to go, if ' anything like pleasure is sought, or if the fact that one is living in California is to be realized. City life is, I guess, much the same all the world over, but this place has one notorious feature which makes it par excellent amongst cities. I say notorious, because the feature I refer to has such a disagreeably homely character. The city is literally INFIISTED WITILFLNAS. Readers of the " Examiner " would smile to hear the flea anecdotes told here every day. In public meetings, at the theatre or at church, what shrug- ging of shoulders there is All sort of antics and devices are resorted to with the fell intent of dis- turbing the lively flea; the- monsters will in spite of it all—
Strike home, gash deeps. The wound, will itch, and leave behind a scar.

The other night the Dame was flea catching, but the monotonous crack, crack sent me to sleep after I heard her say—" There that is thirty-five fleas. I'll give it up for to-night? I was soon roused by some one else in another room calling out, " Ma, we 1-illed ever seventy." The usual and surest method of flea catching is to stand up to the knees in water in a bath, but give sundry good shakes and listen to the flop, flop as the poor doomed insects meet their untimely end. The trouble is, while we can leave the penetrating flea to the city, we find in the coun- try the piercing mosquitoes. Blood seems to be the chief article in demand in the Californian insect world. What reason there may be for this I cannot say, but anyho iv it must be a one-skied rea- son for the genus homo has in this part of the world no blood to spare, unless it might be in defence of the " Stars and Stripes" against you" domed Britishers." Well, I got out of the city and away from its hard-shelled jumpers, and came at last to understand that California had in it some nice coun- try lanes, through which one could walk with plea- sure. Lanes winding through MILES UPON MILES OIP ORCIIA.RDS.

On every side were trees laden with fruit of all kinds, peaches, apricots, plums, and fruits of which we didn't know the name. It was quite a treat to my daughter flarrie and I to walk the lanes of Fruit Vale. I vow it is the first walk and the first real view of a bit of country since we left home. Still, there is something about it which makes the country not to be compared with one I know of. The lanes are covered with a dry clinging dust which covers the pedestrian until he looks like one in a snowstorm. The fields are brown and literally dried up, looking as if green things would never again show above the surface. For seven months in the year not a drop of rain falls, and all becomes dry and arid. I is always safe to make arrange- ments for picnics within certain dates, toad this is the land of picnics. Of course this does well for fruit growing, although I am clear that California fruit is not to be coMpared with fruit grown in the eastern states, and in Europe. Walking through Fruit Vale, we reached Beulah Park where we struck

WHEN Lucy Layton was informed of the sad and sudden death of poor George Collier, she first experi- enced a sense of relief, but this selfish feeling did not last long. She recalled all his tenderness and love in the old days, his constancy and friendship in the later times; the kind heart and simple faith which had made him ever welcome to all, and the tears started to her eyes. She felt she would never have such a friend again. It is always thus. When we have a friend we do not value him or her—the old parallel can be drawn daily. We do not care for what we possess, but when we lose it we feel the want at it—no matter what it may be, money, friendship, or love. How is it possible that such a Iscl an my son can, have been born, of such a mother? Lady Deane isthozoughbred to theback- bone, The boy—God forgive me—is a cad! I can't help saying. it, Rushleigh. Ife is not gentleman." "I think you have been expecting too much," replied the captain. "The youth is not a bad fellow, en far as I can see. He is shy and reserved—pars- , sionate you will, bait wants leading. A gentle firm hand would bring him round. He is not had look- ing; be is tall and strong, and in excellent condi- tion. Ti he were my son I would send him to college, or some large public school." "Yes, you are right, Rushleigh ; I have been ex- pecting too much. I have pinned my heart so to that lad that I any rightly punished for my selfish- ness. Yea; he shall go to a public school and forget all about this Minnie Collier girl" Rushleigh was on the point if mentinning the great likeness which existed betneen her and tho General, but he refrained. He ditermlned to ascer- tain the' origin of this curious coitteldence and with that object he sought an interviear with Akinnio ha the Wise.

div.p: But 14 the time he had soothed his old friend and hound himself at liberty to question the young lady he found she had been sent home in charge of one of the servants, and all he could do was to ask where - was to be found. _

General Deane, at dinner that evening, communi- cated to his wife, and indirectly to his son, his newly- made determination to send the' latter to school or college, and the young man registered a mental vow to ran away sooner than be so humiliated! Was he who had been educated at home by a long-suffering tutor' and permitted to have all his own way when- ever he pleased; was he tobo sent to college, when he would bei put under restraint, and made to learn " beastly " Latin aLI Greek l "Not much," ho said to himself.t 'Then another brilliant idea struck him. He might certainly rim away, but what if bet carried Minnie with him?. AU was fair in war and love. Minnie might be induced to meet him, and then he fancied he could persuade her to marry hirn, for, selfish as MarmadulFe Deane was, he was honourably disposed to the girl, and really intended to make her his wife. He trusted:to time to create an affection for him if he could only persuade her to leave home. Humility and penitence were his best cards, and these he determined to play at first. He had no real doubt respecting be eventual aocoptance of his overtures when she :found no immediate escape. $o the only difficulty Marina- duke had to encounter was the attendance of the girl at the place he intended to meet her. Perhaps he could enlist her mother in the plot- She was quite willing to let him marry Minnie. H his own plan failed, he would request Mrs. Layton to use her parental authority. Meantime he made his preparations secretly. He packed up some things, and put by all his ready money. By degrees, as Ile had a handsome anew- ante, he managed to save a considerable sum, and he found to his hands an easy tool in the person of "Sandy" Sam, who was rawly and willing to perpo, trate any act of villainy if he were only paid. suffir eiently high. While Marneaduke and his4elly: were plotting the abduction of the innocent Minnie Layton, she' was busily engaged in shaping her own destiny—quite independently of mother or father. The old story scarcely needs telling. She had made her choice, and the devotion of young Watson had touched her , heart. He had sought her love, declared his passion, and thus, unknown to all but him, Minnie had plighted her troth to Edward Watson,

CHAPTER XXL AN AMB7BII AND A DISCOTERT. Wl'rumE nissed her "Uncle George" veryg mum"— He appeared to her in the light ot at parent t-Atue lboked up to him for advice and. assistance, and, when she saw her dear "uncle," as she persisted int calling him„ carried, to the little churchyard, her griei knew no bounds. For the first time in her lifeshe thendelt the want ofat companion, and, her heart desired a confidEsat. • This said that when an engagement between two, young people has been broken off, and

- - - - "Alas I how light a calms may move Dissection between hearts that that-they are more prone to attach tharaselvesqb other " afflnitiee" after such a rupture. My own experience does' not warrant me in under-writing this statement, but it has been said so, and a gixl once deprived of her lover will cast her tendrils upon some °then object, as the ivy turn from one place will cling-to another, and grow up sTeenunil,

strong again. Mind, I do wet commit myself to this theory as, exemplified in humanity. I only give it expression. and think it probable. At any rate Minnie found herself very lonelyafter poor "Uncle George' died, and her usual walk to the eignal.leox or along the line, or, better still, along_ the wide-spreading. sands with George Collier were, all at anJend. Her mother, too, felt the loss she had etistained, and WBlO3 reserved and silent. But the return of the General had a good deal to da with, that.

How could slie promote her plan? Minnie abso- lately refused to see Marmadulce Deane. She "bated. him," she said, and all the representations .Mrsp. Layton could make were disregarded. One day Lucy came in, terror in her face. She had seen a ghost! There could be no' mistake. It had appeared to herin a small path where there was no escape to the right hand or to the left. She was permed in , like the animal on which Balaam rode, and she almost fell down from sheer terror. Bu unlike the ass, she did not speak, and the figure disappeared. When shseame home she told her" daughter" that she intended .to leavethe cottage, unless she (Minnie) would consentto see Marraaduke Deane, and endes4 Tour to school herself ta his addresses.

Minnie declin.ed firmly, and an animated :discuss elan and scene of recrimination arose, in the midst. of which the,girlleft the house in a flood of team, and carrying all her ready money in her pocket, and a small bundle, declared she would put up with such I 1 persecution no longer. She would seek General Deane and ask his advice. She was running into tlaelion's mouth, for" Sandy" Sam had carried her a pencilled note, signed E. W. begging her to come to the corner.of the wood ead. consult about their prospects. "Hwill tell me what to do," she thought "I: can go with him if he likes to take me. I cannot stop at home and he persecuted day after day about that horrible man.. lie shall decide." Of course. all this was very unconventional. ' Minnie ought to, bam known better, but she had ' not had thsadvantages of the School Board education, and wes moreover somewhat self-willed. So she ran away to escape Mrs. Layton's importunities, yet, lilts another young lady, who is in ray mind as I write, she fell" from the frying pan into the fire." "Sandy." Sam had, in conjunction with the in,. fatuated Marmaduke, laid his plans well. Minnie had crushed the note as soon as she had glanced at it, too greatly agitated 4.,4, remark the very "scribbleds' manner in which it was written. Her brain. WS busied with one idear—to escape Marma— duke and b.r "mother's" pleading and imper tunitiee.in.hisfeyour. She fell, into the trap. bfarmaduke waswaiting for her.-in, the isomer of the wood. "Sandy" Sam, was closeby.. Minnie turnedopale and then:red at. she guessed:the note was a forgery. "o glad you have come, ,Minnie," said Marme: duke respectfully enough. "-I did not expect you. so scan.. Sam, you needn't wait close. I wish tc. speak..to. Mho Layton." "Sandy" Sam withdraw -to, a discreet. distancet and watched the pair intently. " do you mean, to say you vrrots. that notnon purpose to draw use out here "..Fmtlfraid I did, Minnie, but you see I had,nc ebldee. and you are prepared to comaowith, mei. I see.'

"-Do yen? Then loturte tell you I rover expeated tzo sief you, and don't war..t to eithar. So lam punished enough already. Now, dou't detairome; uorChdare to touch She drew herself to her frill height,and, young as One was, there was, a dignity about her which Idarmaduke recognised, and made him, unfortu- nately, admire her all tho more. "I don't want to hurt you, Dlinnic , I have your mother's consent to marry you. Sc,l will_ You will consent, won't you ?"

"Listen, Mr. Deane. If there was not another man in the world .I wouldn't marry, you. I detest you, particularly since you have persectrWd me so. Why can't you,leavo ate alone? lam going to the Ball now, so let me poss." Marmaduke had flushed angrily at the ceaxterep*, expressed for him, and had faced her on,the narrow Path. "Now listen to 4113, Miss Minnie. Yen shall marry me by fair means. if%you will—by foul means if you will not. My plans can't give way to yours. I love yon and have made up my mind to have you for my wife. So come along, No screaming or yon, will repent it." "And this is your love, is.itP To.earr, a girl off by force! rll die first. Help! Help!" " Ah, youmoy scream; nobody erBI hear you now. It's too late. Here, Sam, just tear a hand, will you? She's uncommon strong "

Sam approached, and Minnie), with a sinking heart and half-fainting with terror, had still pre. sence of mtnil enough to, perceive that re:date/ice was useless.. "Don't touch me," she cried.. " Stand aside, you eowards. Oh! if George Collier was alive, he'd soon put you out of sight. What do you, want?" "Corn, with me. My trap is waiting.. I sweal interd you no injury. Consent to be my wife, and I will to content. I will do you no violence Rut min!: you shall be. I can't do without you Minnie, do be reasonable ! " She looked at him alrooot in pity. Ile had lost all his high tone, and had already began to plead. Thera was hope yet. Deane—Marmaduke—l will call you so you like. We used to be friends. I used to like you, but lately you have become quite different. You are a gentleman, born and bred. lam only a cottage girl; yet when I tell you. I cannot love you— " Because you love Edward Watson, I suppose,* he said, roughly. "Yes, I do, and tre are engaged. Now, Mr. Deane.

you see how impossible it is- that I can marry yon. You may carry me off, and perhaps reader me —I can't tell; but you cannot make me love you. 1 could like you, but you are so different." "I wish you were, Minnie," he said, more gently. " Marmaduke—Mr. Deane—do have pity on me. I am driven away from home on your account. Mother is always at me to marry you. I can't. I won't— rd rather die!" , "You must, Minnie, I can't bear to lose YOU. I am a fool," he burst out violently. "BY Gad, you nearly talked me over. No, I'm not such a fool as to give you up now I have done all this! It's getting dark, ray lady," he continued, suddenly changing his tone, "and before daylight comes again you and I will be far away from here. Come, no yelling, or, by Jingo, I'll gag you!" He seized her in his powerful arms as he spoke, and ere she was scarcely aware of his intention he had carried her into the wood far from the footpath. She screamed as loudly as she could, but Sandy Sam, who was less scrupulous than his employer, thrust a handkerchief tightly into her mouth and nearly suffocated her. In the grasp of Marmaduke Deane she was now quite helpless, and in five minutes he • had carried her to a small hut once used for shelter of peat cutters in the adjacent swampy ground. , The seizure had been so suddenly made that poor Minnie had not an opportunity of defending herself, and now she was quite helpless. A bandage wee placed over her eyes, and in a semi-unconscious condition she was, after a pause for rest, carried and partly dragged through the wood to some place where a horse and trap were waiting. She recognised the champing of ths bit, suvnese that she wasP about to be carried away.. Marufeduke Deane was panting with passion and extitement. He had gone too far to retract, and he knew it. He must now go through the job in any case, and carry her away out of the country and aoress the sea before daylight Minnie felt a cold chill come over her, and. with a deep sigh she fell back in her abductor's arms insensible. "Now's the time," said Sandy Sam.. "Get her into the cart and away with you. She's fainting. You'll find the beat ready at the creek yonder. There is plenty to eat in the little hut on the hill- ;side. No one ever goes up there now; there's nothing to be shot,. I suppose. Be off, and geed. luck to you. Here's her bundle. I'll follow ye and take the trap.' Marmaduke, scarcely believing that h 3 had Elo easily succeeded, and yet dreadfully alarmed at the success of his plans, did not wait to say good-bye. He laid the poor girl gently down, and, getting into the phton, drove rapidly away. In about half-an-hour he reached the creek, and found the boat ready. The night was calm and still. Not a soul was near, and the wretched man half lifted, half assisted the almost inanimate form from the seat upon which she reclined and put her into the stern sheets of the boat. He had, however, to lay her down as Minnie was still helpless, and, cursing his luck, he pushed the boat nearly out, when lie remembered he had not fastened the horse's bridle. He leaped ashore, and tied the animal to the , adjacent paling. Not a minutelwas expended in the process, and then, with a hasty step and bestial' heart, he turned to the boat again. • But the boat and Minnie had both disappears&

HOW A GOOD SHIP WAS LOST.

On the night of October 27th, 1842, the good ship "Mary Compton," of Bristol, England, was struggling with& fearful gale off the coast of North America. The 'wind blew furiously, but the weather was clear, and the Captain expected every moment to get sight of the light in the lighthouse on the Iron Rock Shoals. This light- house marked the entrance to the harbour. Once there, and they were safe. Sure of his position, he sailed on confidently. Five minutes later the ship struck with a fearful shock and went to pieces. Four men, including the captain, were saved. On reaching the shore they found a strange thing had happened. An enemy of the lighthouse keeper had bound him hand and foot and extinguished the light. Souls, as well as ships, steer by the lights. Hope is The most important lighthouse in the world. What shall be said of the man who darkens it in the face of a storm - tossed spirit? "You .are beyond human aid." These words were said by a physician to a woman who had come to consult him. Admitting that he thought so, had he the right to say so? No, for he might be wrong—and in any case he had no business to put out the light. This woman had been ill for some time. In June, 1889, She was greatly alarmed by her symptoms. Her heart palpitated, and she was so giddy she could scarcely

stand. Her head whirled " and she said, "all objects seemed to go into a cloud." She had to hold herself up IV sit down for fear of falling. She broke out in a sweat although cold as death. A dreadful cough racked

tter frame so that she could not lie down iu bed and sleep. "I could scarcely crawl about the house," she says, I was so weak. I tried different remedies and medi- cines without avail. I went to the Dispensary at New
----- Briggate and asked the doctor to tell me the worst. His -• •
answer was I have mixed you some medicine ; you can take it or leave it.' I took it for three weeks, and then gave up in despair. I talked with two other physicians,
- _ The last one said, You are past hvlrsan aid.

"My heart sank within me, for I had five little children, end my death would leave them without a mother's love and care. I went home and cried till I was sick. I had no appetite and had lost flesh till I icas thin as a ghost ! Ily mother came to see me and did not know me. My akin was of a green and yellow colour, and when I ate anythihg it seemed to stick in my throat. About this
_ time I commenced vomiting, and what I threw up was

tinged with blood One I began to vomit at nine o'clock on a Saturday morning, and scarcely got rest from it Until Monday morning. At this time I remembered that Mrs. Wilson, with whom I formerly worked in Crawford's Mill, in East Street, Leeds (where I live), had been cured by Mother Seigel's Curativesyrup. So I sent to Mr. Jesson's the chemist, in Great Garden Street, and got a bottle. A few doses stOpped the vomiting, and by degrees from day to day I felt better. Soon I could eat a dry crust, and by the time I had finished the second bottle I had gut over all my bad symptoms, and was fast getting my strength back. lam now (April, 1890) in better health than ever before in my life.

"I should have taken Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup sooner, but my husband was out of work, and we had only a trifle coming in from his club. But I thank God I did get it at last, and it cured me, bad off as I was. All any friends and neighbours know the facts I have related and I will reply to any letters of inquiry." (Signed), Mrs. Ann Mills, 40, Bread-street, York-road, Leeds. This was a case of indigestion and dyspepsia, with Symptoms showing how far it had affected the nervous System. A few months, or possibly weeks more, and Mrs. Mills would have had no tale to tell. She did wrong to wait one hour for any reason, after having known what Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup had done for her friend Mrs Wilson.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

VIOLENT ASSAULT. On Saturday, at the Warrington Police Court, a rough looking young man named Odlaghan was brought up in custody on charges of having violently assaulted Constable Clough, and a youth named Samuel Sutcliffe, a hawker. The latter complained to the police of having been assaulted, and on apprehension, prisoner kicked Clough. It was his 30th appearance, and he was sent to Prison for six weeks. • A BP.ICK-ST FIGHT. , On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, Charles, John, and Henry Derbyshire brothers, and Alfred Hargreaves, were summoned for having disturbed the peace by fighting in Brick-st, on the 31st September. There appeared to have been something like a general fight, and the cases had been before the court on a Previous occasion, but were adjourned for it to be a,scertained who were really at fault. Henry Derbyshire Was dismissed, and the other defendants were bound over to be of good behaviour.

ALLEGED ROBBERY WITT( VIOLENCE AT WARRINGTON. At Warrington, on Monday afternoon, two young men, named George Wicks and William Farrell, described as labourers, were brought before a county magistrate at the Occasional Court on a charge of having stolen 125., '•%, with violence, from the person of Fred Brain, a Ship Canal t engine-driver, who lives at one of the Acton Grange huts. The prosecutor alleged that when going through Arpley Fields, late on Saturday night, he was accosted, knocked down, and robbed of his cash. Suspicion fell upon the prisoners, but the magistrate was of epinion that the case ^ had not been made out against them, and therefore they - were dismissed.
THEFT OF A VEST

_ On Tuesday, at the Warrington Police Court, Walter Whitley (22), who has for a short time been lodging at 80, Mersey-st., Warrington, pleaded guilty to a charge of having stolen a moleskin vest, of the value of 3s. 6d., from the shop of William Leslie, second-hand clothes - dealer, 65, Mersey-st. Constable Critehley met the prisoner, and noticing that his appearance was bulky he stopped and questioned him. The officer then found -• that the prisoner had the vest concealed under a portion of his clothing, and taxed him with having stolen it. At first prisoner met the charge with a denial, but the P• inquiries instituted by the police showed that the vest had been stolen from the shop of the prosecutor.--The magistrates sent Whitley to prison for two months, with hard labour. UNHAPPY MARRIED Lis'. At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday morning, "t‘ Elliott Gardner, or Gordon, a watchmaker, appeared to answer a summons, charging him with having com- mitted an aggravated assault upon his wife., on the sth October. Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the prose- !, cutrix, said that the charge arose out of a family matter. • Owing to the unhappy circumstances that had taken place during the married life of the couple' and owing to - the fetrful tionduct of the defendant, he had consented to a conviction being recorded against him for an ag- gravated assault, to be bound over in his own recogni- sauces for twelve months, and to pay his wife 7s. 6d. a week under a judicial separation order. The wife was going home tc Birmingham with her father, and the de- fendant had accepted the conditions named. He was accordingly bound over.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATVEDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley, Councillor Voisev, and Mr.R. Garnett. DRITNICENNESS.—For this offence David Wood was fined 53. and costs.—Patrick Moore, charged with drunkenness, in Winwick-st., was fined 53. and costs.—Annie Cart- wright, charged with a similar offence, was sent to prison for a month with hard labo or. CLAIM AGAIIIST A WORKlEAN.—Griffith Griffiths was , summoned by Messrs. R. Garnett.and C 0.., who claimed £1 15s. from defendant on account of his having left Work without notice. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence. Mr. Garnett said that it was the custom of his aStablishment that a week's notice should be given, and he did not wish the rules to be broken. Mr. Browne said that the rules of the jolnering trade were that notice of two hours only should be given on either side. Defendant was a joiner, and was a member of a Union that required that he should follow out that custom. On the suggestion of the Bench, Mr. Garnett withdrew the claim, Mr. Browne also withdrawing a counter-claim for 4s. 6d. made by the defendant. MONDAr.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), Alderman Sutton, Alderman Harrison, and Captain Nicholson. DRUNICENNESS.—For this offence the following persons were dealt with :—James Curley, in Howley-fields, fined S. and costs ; John Bevan, in Buttermarket-st., fined including costs ; Thomas Carleton, in Horsemarket- ;'t, fined 55., including costs ; and Alice Potts, in San- !'el,-st., fined Sc.,including costs : Margaret Gibbons, 44 Old-road, Latchford, dismissed with a caution.

div.p: CHIMNEYS ON FIRE.--Thomas Kiinblin was fined Is. for having allowed his dwelling-house chimney to be on fire.—Robert Coltart, of Queen-A., was charged with a similar offence, and the officer who gave evidence said he found the room where the fireplace was strewed with burned paper, wood, and shavings. He was offered is. not to report the matter. A fine of ss. was imposed. STONE TanowlNG.—Percy Mather, Charles Ashton and Williana Dunbobbin, boys, were each fined Is. for throw- ing stones on Liverpool-road, on the 29th September. DRIVERS FlNED.—Patrick Martin was fined 55., includ- ing costs, for having obstructed Horsemarket-st, near Market-gate, for a longer period than was necessary, on the 27th September.—Peter Cartledge, for furiously driving a pony and cart in Butterrnarket-st., on the 30th September, was fined 55., including costs.—Wm. Rowles, for a similar offence, on the 29th September, was fined in a like amount. A Doci AT LARGE.—James Kenyon, for allowing a dog to be at large unmuzzled on the 26th September, was lined 2s. 6d. and costs. TURSDAL—Before Messrs. R. Garnett and E. M. t"..

div.head: Crosfield.
div.p: Crosfield.

DRUNKENNESS'—Robert Daniek, for this offence, was fined be. and costs.—A man named Morgan, for a similar offence, was ordered to pay costs. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—SeveraI persons were summoned for neglecting to regularly send their children to school, the cases being proved by Mr. George Riley, the School Attendance Officer. WHDNBSDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough, Alderman _ _

Chandley and Mr. E. J. Nicholson. DRIINISENNH3S, &c.—James Power, in Cairo-st., on Tuesday night,fined ss. including costs . • James Mc righe, drunk and disorderly on Town Hill and assaulting P.C. Faulkner, fined 10s. and costs or 14 days. ASSAULT.—A young man named Harrop Chadwick, was charged with having assaulted a woman in Butter- market-st., on the previous night, and she was bound over to keep the peace. ~..F.RlDAY.—Before Mr. Jmhn Platt and Dr. Gomall. BEGGING.—Thomas Cunningham, brought up in cus- tody on a charge of haying asked alms in Manchester- road, was discharged for want of eyidence.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
.....,......., - MONDAY.—Before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. James

Handley. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Michael Phillips, Mersey-st., was ordered to pay 9s. for permitting the chimney of his dwelling to be on fire. SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—Runcorn School Board sum- moned a number of parents for not sending their chil- dren regularly to school and on the evidence of Mr. Bowyer were each fined ss. and costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence Ellen Bar- ker, and Robert Ridley, were each fined ss. and costs and Michael Curley, Thomas Young and Robert Thompson were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs. ASSAULTING A CHlLD.—William Williams an old man-, was summoned with assaulting George William Martin, a boy 4 years of age. It was alleged that a number of children were " playing school" in the street, when the , defendant threw a stick amongst them and struck the boy on the face. He was under the care of the doctor.— The defendant said a number of big lads kicked at his door, and threw stones into the house, and also called him names. He threw a small stick after them and the small boy happened to be amongst them.—The Bench said he had no doubt received much provocation, and ordered him to pay the costs ss. 6d. STREET OBSTRUCTION.—WiIIiam Wilkinson, William Raynor, and Alfred Mills were each summoned for ob- structing the footpath at Delph Bridge, on Sunday the 28th September.—Superintendent Large said he had received many complaints of this nuisance, and the defendants had been warned several times.—They were each ordered to pay 4s. 6d. costs. CRUELTY TO A PONY—Edward Prince was summoned for cruelly illtreating a horse by causing it to be worked in an unfit state, on the 17th September. Inspector Wilson, R.5.0.C.A., deposed to seeing the defeadant's pony drawing a cart. The animal was in low condition, was excessively lame on theoff hind leg, and was totally unfit for work.—lnspector Bowyer and P.C. Woodrow corroborated.—The defendant said he had worked the pony for fifteen months, and had never received any complaint before. He contended that it was quite fit to work. Mr. Reynolds said the prosecution ought to have brought a veterinary surgeon to prove the state ot the horse. The defendant must pay 7s. 6d. and costs.— Inspector Wilson said the inspectors had all to pass a veterinary examination before they were appointed. This was a simple case in which they did not think it i necessary to put the society to the expense of a veteri- nary surgeon. BAD LANGUAGE.—Robert Houghton, a young man, I was fined ss. and costs for using obscene and profane language.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS,
THITRSDAY.—Before Mr. H. _ Gasket! and Lieu.-Colonel
Gaskell.

MiscaLzaNaous.—For being drunk and disorderly a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Charles Ducker, William Henry Roseve, Alice Drewry, William Glasheen, Julia Doyle. For a similar offence Elizabeth Glashe,en, Benjamin Dignam, Christopher Daley, were each fined 7s. 6d. and costs.—Margaret McCann, Harriet Burns, Mary Wharton, Joseph Hoban. Annie Gallagher, and John Ducker were sum- moned for creating a breach of the peace, and were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months.— John Halton. of Major Cross-st., was fined is. and costs for having his chimney on fire.—Elizabeth Glasheen, of Caroline-st., was summoned for assaulting Christopher , Daley by striking him on the head with a boot, and she was fined ss. and costs—total 1 ss. 6d. CRUELTY TO A HEN.-Wm. Fay, of Eleanor-st., Wid- nes, was charged with cruelly illtreating a hen at Dit- ton on the 19th ult. Inspector Wilson R.S.F.C.A. prosecuted. The hen, which belonged to Mrs. Wird was feeding on some waste land, at Ditton, when the defend- ant kicked it, and broke its neck, and the thigh of the right leg. The fowl died a minute or two later. The defendant, who did not appear was fined 2s. 6d. and costs or 14 days imprisonment in default.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

**. Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

MATTO HEATH V. LITTIERLAND.—The fixture between these teams was played on Saturday, and the boys from the Heath were victorious by 1 goal, 2 tries and 3 minors to nil. Sr. HELENS OLD Boys v. LOWTON.—Lowton paid a visit to the Old Boys, on Saturday, for the first time. The Boys were victorious by 1 goal 1 try and 2 minors, to 1 try and 3 minors. ST. HELENS (A) V. TRANMERE WANDERERS.—The above teamsmet on Saturday, at Birkenhead. When time was up St. Helens were victors of a rough game by 1 goal 1 try and 6 minor, to Tranmere, 3 tries and 5 minors. WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND Y. WIGAN RECREATION IST. --The above teams met at Warrington, on Saturday, the home team standing no chance against their smart oppo- nents, who ran out winners to the tune of 1 goal, tries, 5 minors to nil. Fairhurst, Sutton, Rafferty, and Green scored for the winners. WARRINGTON RANGERS V. TNELWALL HORNETS.—This match took place on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and the game, which was chiefly of a forward nature, resulted in a victory for the Rangers by 2 goals, 1 try, 3 minors, to the Hornets 1 minor. Kenwright, Ashton, and O'Brien secured tries for the winners, Morrall and Potts kicking the goals, ST. HELENS T. WALKDEN.—St. Helens played their second League match of the season on Saturday, their opponents being Walkden, and in this they sustained defeat. The Committee of the Club decided to give half the proceeds to the funds of the men on strike at Pilking- tons', and as a consequence there was a larger attend- ance of spectators than usual, over 2,000 Unit'," the enclosure. Both clubs had representative teams. lining thirty-fives were agree upon, and Walkden put the ball in motion, with the wind against them. Exchanges followed and the game was evenly contested until Vickers (Walkden) received the ball in mid-field, and took a drop at goal which was successful. The game was afterwards hotly contested but the visitors won by a drop goal and four minors to three minors. Ru•semot V. OLD EDWARDlANS.—Saturday's engage- ment at Runcorn was with the Old Edwardians, and the game was one of much interest. A strong team re- presented Birmingham whilst Runcorn was without the services of H. Hughes, Hughes, Faulkner, T. Davies, and J. Davies. The ball was put into motion by Adams, on behalf of the Old Edwardians, and the home quarters were determinedly attacked. Here the services of Cromp- ton were turned to good account, and he relieved the pressure. Badger then received a pass from Adams, and there were signs of danger; but Houghton saved by punting into touch. Both teams then warmed to their work, the forwards on both sides working most energeti- cally. P. Riley made the most of an opportunity which presented itself • but he was brought down by Moore on the line, another minor resulting. Gayter, who was on the alert, rushed the sphere to the centre of the ground,. and Abrams came to the rescue, and succeeded in crossing the line at the corner; but the goal kick failed. Then Moore, from a line out, received the ball and got over ' • but again the kick at goal was a failure. At half time Runcora's score was two tries two minors ; Edwardians, nil. After the usual interval, the ball was set in motion by Broady, but was worked into touch. Passing of a most meritorous character succeeded this, Crompton, Abrams, and May being engaged in it, and the result was. that the latter crossed the line, but the goal was a failure. Moore almost immediately after- wards got over, and the same misfortune followed ; but from the kick-out Badger for the visitors put in a splen- did run, and then followed some good passing; but Crompton relieved. Crompton, from a pass by Abrams, dropped a splendid goal, and shortly afterwards gave the visitors a great deal of trouble, and after a most excit- n g run he placed the ball behind the posts, and succeeded in kicking a goal. At the close of play the score was— Runcorn, 2 goals, 2 tries, 5 minors ; Old Edwardians, ST. HELENS RECREATION V. BAmzow.—These teams met

div.head: 4100! – , THE EXAMINER, " SATIT.RDA_Y, OCTOBER 11, 1890.

at S. Helens, on Saturday and were as follows :—Recrea- tion : T. R. Jackson, full back ; J. Ellison. J. Seddon, and J. Fairclough, three-quarters ; J. Pilkington, and J. Turton, half backs; Sr Parr, J. Dolan, J. Mousdale, J. Hankinson, P. Fildes, W. Dean, A Tickle' W. Cliffe, and R. Fildes forwards. Barrow : Airey, full blck : Milner (capt.), Laughton, and Barnett, three-quarters ; Dickenson and Leake, half back ; Greaves, Jackson, Powell, Garner, Balsa, Cowell, Harley, Blezard, and Dickinson, forwards. The Recs. won the toss' Cowell started play for the visitors. Before the game had been proceeding many minutes, Seddon took a pass from PH- kington, dodged through the whole pack, and planted the oval near to the posts. From the place he kicked the goal, and a few minutes later Puking. 1 ton got possession from a scrimmage, and was over' again. The kick at goal was from the corner and the leather was carried just outside the posts. Shortly afterwards Pilkington passed to Fairclough who got over in the corner, and Seddon again failed to con- vert. From a scrimmage in front of the goal, Dolan passed to Parr who transferred to Seddon, and he made another exciting run through the pack, and completed the try. The place kick was entrusted to Ellison who failed. Fairclough again got over but the place kick by Seddon again failed. Half time was then called with the score a goal, four tries and seven minors for the Recs, and nothing for Barrow. Seddon kicked off in the second hslf, but Barrow pressed and after some scrimmaging in the home half Harley trotted over. Milner, who last season kicktclls goals out of 16 attempts, failed at this one. Shortly afterwards Dickenson, got possession in front of the posts and dropped a goal. The visitors continued to play up well for a time, and made several dangerous raids on the home goal, but the homesters subsequently pressed and Hankinson and Pilkington scored tries and Seddon kicked a goal. The Recreation, 2 goals, 5 tries, and 9 minors. Barrow, 1 goal and 1 try. WIDNES v. ROCHDALE ST. CLEMENTS.—RochdaIe St. Clement's met Widnes on the ground of the latter at loowerhouse-lane, on Saturday afternoon, before about 2,000 spectators. The visitors brought with them a strong team, but Widnes was only poorly represented, Plumpton, Brennan, and Gordon being absent, while the men gene:ally seemed totally unfit for the fight which was to follow. Smith started the ball against the wind, , and after some give-and-take play, Foster failed to return, and the ball was kicked dead to save disaster. Si. Clement's after the drop out continued to press, but Peters and Clarke succeeded in equalizing matters. A few minutes later Hyde got possession and got over, but the kick at goal failed. Rochdale St. Clements, appar- ently encouraged by this pie de of good luck played with a still greater dash, :and completely baffed the Widnes players. Coyne crossed the line, but Foster saved just in the nick of time. The play of Widnes was constantly on the defensive, and several times minors had to be conceded to bring the ball out of danger. At half time Rochdale St. Clement's had I scored one try and four minors to Widnes nil. On changing ends hopes were entertained that, with the winclin their favour Widnes would make a much better I show, but in this the spectators were doomed to dis- appointment. They commenced the second half with an attack on the visitor's line, in which Peters and Hartles I were conspicuous, but after some even play, they were repulsed to their own quarter, and compelled to resort to 'defensive tactics. Peters and Clarke tackled well, and with the assistance of Dummqnd, Johnson, and Whelan, the ball was brought to centre again. This play was followed up a few passes between Peters, Clarke, and Hartles, which proved a slight gain, but having lost possession again, Widnes were compelled to beat a hasty retreat. Here a minor was scored by St. Clement's, and immediately after the drop out Holt for Rochdale got possession, and scored a splendid try, from which a goal was kicked. The remainder of the game was of an even nature' and when the whistle blew the score was Roch- dale St. Clements, one goal, one try, and five minors, to Widnes, nil. Teams :—Widnes: Forster, back; Peters, Clarke, and Hartles, three-quarter backs ; Drummond and Howard, half-backs; Smith, Holt, Farmer, Hewitt, Johnson, Stubbs, Carroll, Whelan, and Laws, forwarus. Rochdale St. Clement's : Rigg, back; Hyde, Barton, and Thompson, three-quarter backs ; Heywood and Coyne, half back ; W. Waugh J. Waugh, Farron, Holt, Hill, Dex, Connor, B. Rideheough, and R. Rideheough, for- wards.

WARRINGTON A v. BROUGHTON A.—The Warrington- ians journeyed to Broughton, on Saturday, to fulfil this engagement, which was played before a small but select company. The visitors started uphill, and against a stiffish breeze, and at once rushed to the home quarters, and when looking dangerous. Nelsen averted disaster in daring fashion. The oval was not destined to remain here long, for a free kick to the Broughtenians relieved their lines and took play to the Warrington quarter flag. Fast play was the order, until a pass from Davies to Jolley enabled the latter to punt well into his opponents' territory. After some tall exchanges had been indulged in by the rival backs, Jolley got finally away, and pass- ing to Daniels, the leather was taken to midfield. Directly after this a long kick by A. Smith enabled his side to put in a fierce attack on the Warrington lines, but after it had been successfully beaten off, and Law- less, Knowles, and Beard had cleared their lines, a grand run by Bate entirely changed matters, and passing to Lawless the latter scored, which Webster converted. From the kick off Jolley put in a splendid piece of work, but eventually Broadbent, Wilde, and Budgeon dribbled well into their antagonists' territory, when Webster saved. From this point the game entirely changed, the Warrington backs playing a magnificent game. A fine piece of work by Webster, the same player tackling the home full back on his likes, gained considerable ground, and Bate passing to Lawless, another try was obtained. Following the drop out Mather passed to Bate, who put in a magnificent run and almost scored. A. Smith re- lieved by a long kick, and Turner, when looking danger- ous, was grandly tackled by Davies. Some good forward play by Isherwood, Russell, Warburton, and Barnes en- sued, and the result of some capital passing by Lawless' Mather, Jolley, and Daniels was a try to Mather's credit. Sampson returned the drop out finely, and directly after- wards, a long run and kick by Webster resulted in Beard scoring. The drop out failed to clear the Broughton lines, the passing of their opponents being irresistible, and Webster obtained a splendid try, whilst immedi- ately afterwards Daniels secured one, the score at half- time reading 1-5-0 to nil. Restarting, Sampson was early prominent by a splendid run and kick, and from a pass Jolley made a grand run right through his op- ponents and Daniels got another try under the posts. A le* minutes after this Bate got possession, and feigning to pass ran clean under the posts, Davies converting both tries. The remaining portion of the ..ame was of a too one-sided nature to describe, suffice to say that three tries were obtained by Webster, the final reading—War- rington 4-7-3 to nil. Teams: Warrington: Sampson, back ; Webster, Jolley, and Daniels, three-quarters ; Bate, Lawless, and Mather, half backs; Isherwood, Davies, Molyneaux, Beard, Russell, Warburton, Barnes and Knowles, forwards. Broughton: Shepherd, back; Nelson, Turner, and A. E. Smith, three-quarters ; Wilde, ' and J. Smith, half backs; Broadbent, Corlett, H. H. Smith, Croggan, Anty, Lothian, Morton, Budgeon, and Rodgers, forwards.

being called with the score—Warrington. 0-2-6 : Broughton, nil. On the resumption the visitors at once presented a bold front, and urged on by the few supporters who had accompanied them, it seemed ap- parent that the deficient would soon be wiped off. Bate and Nevins were to the fore with an excellent dribble, only to see a strong movement on the part of Whiteley, Rome, and Dowson, which ended in a minor. Exchange kicking found the oval hovering near the pavilion goal, and after Barnes, Nevins, and Randles had shown rare skill in the passing line, Lawless in his endeavour to punt to his companion three-quarter failed to obtain a proper grip of the oval, with the result that the ball fell at the feet of Wood, who dribbled down the open in fine style, and Flowers Joining issue, a try was placed to the credit of the speedy Broughton three-quarter, McArthur mak- ing a wretched attempt with the place kick. This was Broughton's last chance, for on the restart the ball was quickly worked into Broughton territory, and a passing movement by our local team was eventually stayed by Flowers, who in his anxiety to rid himself of the ball, threw it into the hands of Holmes, and the latter eagerly snapped the opportunity, and scored the third try, Barnes this time placing a goal. The Broughton men were now a beaten team, and this is not to be wondered at, considering the excellent combinaticin they had to contend against. Nevins secured what appeared a clever try, but he had grounded the wrong side of the line, and it was left to Lawless to do the final trick, for securing possession, after some exchanges between Antrobus and Bate, he scored near the corner flag. No goal being placed, a grand game was brought to a conclusion, the final score reading—Warrington, 1-3-6; Broughton,o-1-1. Teams :—Warrington: J. Boscow, back ;P. R. Law- less, T. Barnes, and J. W. Evans, three-quarter backs; J. T. Bate, and W. Antrobus (captain), half backs ; Fair Turner, Frank Turner J. Holmes, W. Nevins, W. Bandies, J. T. Thordey, J. Jolley, B. Berry, and E. Dillon, forwards. Broughton : S. Hassall, back, E. H. Flower, C. Wood, and A. F. McArthur, three-quarter , backs ;W. Whiteley, and S. A. Leathley, half backs ; C. V. Rome. P. lki'Dougal, W. E. Wormald, B. Powell, T. G. Dowson, R. Tomlinson, W. P. Glendinning, A. C. Broadbent, and H. S. Slazinger, forwards.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

Sr. HELENS ASSOCIATION V GOLBORNE.—These teams met at Golborne on Saturday and the match resulted in a somewhat easy win for Golborne by four goals to one. Golborne scored ten minutes after opening play. St. Helens then equalised, but the home team again shot ahead scoring three more goals and winning as above. EARLESTOWN RESERVE V. EARLESTOWN VICTORIA.— These teams met for the first time this season on the ground of the former on Saturday afternoon. Earles- town won the toss, and elected to play for the bottom goal. The Victorians kicked off, and even play resulted for the first quarter of an hour, when Earlestown pressed and shortly after scoring, three goals being added up to half-time. In the second half, the Victorians scored twice, but they were completely overplayed, Earlestown putting on five more goals, ultimately running out winners by 8 goals to 2.—Clarke, Howgace, and Hodnett, showed up best for Earlestown, Whitty and Harrisom being the pick of the Victoria team. EARLESTOWN V. MANCHESTER.—The Earlestown team on Saturday, journeyed to Alexandra Park, to try con- clusions for the first time this season with Manchester, Powell for the home team kicked off before a good num- ber of spectators. The visitors left wing returned the ball, Harrison centred grandly, but the forwards failed to take advantage. Manchester had now a look in, and Wright and Gould experienced hard lines. The home team pressed, but Earlestown clearing made a combined rush for the home goal, but the back division carried play to neutral ground. Give and take play ensued, Wiswell ultimately sending in a stinging shot, which Earp negotiated, a corner shortly afterwards fell to the home team, but proved abortive, a similar point fell to Earlestown, from which Topping scored. This placed the Manchester men en their mettle, and after a scrim- mage in goal Wright equalised. From a corner kick later on Bate registered a second goal, and before half time, Shepperd managed to score again, at half time the score stood, Manchester 3 goals, Earlestown I. On changing ends, Earlestown set the ball rolling, but the home team with combined play placed the visitors goal in danger, giving Bailey and Peet plenty of work. The forwards, however, cleared with a fast dribble down the centre, which resulted in a dead ball. Earlestown still pressed, and after some good play on the part of the front division, Lee scored. From this point Earlestown assumed the upper hand, and the game became fast and exciting. Hard lines,were however,experienced by Earles- town, several shots striking the crossbar and uprights. From a corner kick by Harrison however, Topping headed the ball through equalising matters. Both teams then strained every effort to gain the winning point but nothing further resulted, the game ending in a draw of 3 goals each. Earlestown : H. Johnson, goal; Peet and Bailey, backs ; Bowker, Massey and Wilkinson, half backs ; Lewis, Lee, Topping, Wiswell and Harrison, for- wards. Manchester : Earp, goal; Brookes and Lewis backs; Maddock, Bates and Gould, half backs; Hough- ton, Goswell, Powell, Sheppard and Wright, forwards.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

FOOTBALL—RUGBY. There was a good deal of very fine interesting play on the Wilderspool ground on Saturday. The Broughton team is an improving one and contains some good players. It was pretty clear, however, from the beginning that the Warringtonians were going to have the upper hand. They opened out with great dash and a try with- in two or three minutes of kicking off was not encourag- ing for the visitors. In spite of this the Broughtonians showed no downheartedness and they plryed up to the last minute as though they still had an expectation of turning the tables on the " wirepullers." The home team played a combined game, forward and behind. If there was any weak point it was at half-back. Antrobus and Bate were both sorely hampered by the over-zealous play of their opponents, but still, they might with advantage have fed the three-quarters a little more freely.

The Warrington " A " team still keeps up its conquer- ing career, only more so. The latest score is four goals seven tries and many minors to nil, and it may be taken for granted that the "nil" wasn't on the side of the " champion " A" team." These continual successes have their disadvantages. They get monotonous, and spec- tators don't care much for games when there is only one side in it. An "A " team defeat would be almost a pleasing variation. Perhaps Leigh will oblige.

Swinton were twice beaten by Wigan last year, but on Saturday they partly balanced the account by beatirr, the West Lancashire champions. It was a fierce struggle throughout, both fifteens straining every nerve for the mastery. A goal beautifully dropped by Marsh was the only point in the first half, and a try by Winterbottom the only score in the second, these being all that were recorded. Marsh was in splendid form, and took a vast amount of watching. Valentine, Winterbottom, and Bumby were also very active, whilst among the for- wards Hotchkiss, Hanan, and Walker were often con- spicuous. In future Rugby football, whether for charity or ether purposes, will not be allowed during the close season, a restriction which has been wisely adopted. Nine a-side contests will no longer be tolerated, this being also a much-desired change. Not less than 15 players each side are to be permitted, whatever the object of the match, if gate money is taken. This should put a stop to the pot-hunting which has been so rife in some districts, especially in Yorkshire. - ASSOCIATION. • • -

There has been much commotion in Association circles consequent upon the suspension of Renton. The latter defied the Professional Committee of the Scottish Football Association and played Edinburgh St. Bernards after they had been suspended. Not to be trifled with, the Scotch Association have disqualified Renton until April next. From this it is pretty evident that the Association are determined not to to be, brow-beaten even by such a powerful club as Renton. The Scotch League were generally expected to give Renton their support, but this they have declined, and the case is to be tested in the law courts. Since the suspension became known there has been a great rush by English agents after the unfortunate players.

The League games of Saturday furnished the usual surprise, this being nothing less than the defeat of the champions at , Deepdale., The Blankburn Rovers ' had previously performed so indifferently that no one thought them capable of taking down the North End at Preston, and yet this is What happened. The Rovers won by two goals to one, despite the fact that Douglas was off the field through the second talf. It was a well-earned' vistory; and was much appreciated by the Blackburn. section of the crowd of 10,000. Everton scored their ' fifth consecutive success in the League tourney, finding- an easy prey in Derby County. They have now the splendid record of 23 goals to two. Bolton Wanderers found Aston Villa anything but a formidable team, a poor game ending in the success of the Boltonivis by four points to none. Burnley were vanquished at West Bromwich, the Albion playing well all round. Accring- ton ventured as far as Wolverhampton' where they were not only beaten, but some of the team had their pockets rifled during their absence on the field—an unpleasant experience. -,

The Welsh Football Association on Wednesday night inquired into disturbances which had taken place at cer- tain matches, and it was decided to suspend several players until October 27th. The Committee also passed a resolution making all clubs responsible for the actions of their spectators, unless they could show that they had taken precautions to prevent disturbances.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON.

That a club which play true football are welcome with Warrington audiences was plainly eiddent on Saturday, when Broughton were accorded a hearty reception on making their annual appearance at Wilderspool. It is now fully eight years since the Broughton men first visited this district, then under the name of Mr. Jordan's earn, and it was this match, to the minds of many, that laid the foundation to Warrington's knowledge of the passing game. For that match on Saturday, Broughton brought their best team,whilst the homesters only differed in one respect to that which was originally selected, Holmes taking the place of Ashton, who was indisposed. 'Antrobus, as captain of the home team, won the choice of ends and defended the railway goal, having a light breeze at his back. Flowers' kick off was followed by exchange kicking on the part of Hassell and Nevins, the last-named having slightly the best of it. From a line_ out a sequence of passes between Whiteley, Wood, and McArthur was frustrated by Barnes, and from the second scrimmage of the match the Warrington forwards, working with excellent combination, had are best of the pack, and dribbling effectively through the Brougkton defence, the oval was crossed to Barnes, and a try scored in less than five minutes from the kick off. With Frank Turner failing to increase the point, the drop out was responded to by the last-named player, Jolley, Bandies, and Thornley, each making desperate efforts to notch serviceable scores. Broughton defended admirably, and with less experienced hands than Flowers, Wood, and Co., a heavy score must assuredly have been totalled against them. Evans, by judicious kicking, frequently frustrated an attempt to relieve and from a long kick a minor was conceded. Fair Turner was prominent with a tremendous punt, and although Wood got the oval away to Boscow the last-named was safe as usual,and no anxiety was felt here, the Broughton goal again being endangered from the Warrington custodian's kick. Flowers put in a dodgy run, but his kick was faulty, and then Bate, Antrobus, and Barnes passed finely, a similiar piece of play between Wood and Whiteley chang- ing the venue to the half-way flag. Evans was again responsible for the visitors defending, Barnes following this with one of his characteristic runs falling when scoring seemed within his grasp, Jolley made another effort here, but the tackling was safe, and Berry from a line out ran from the quarter flag, being finally knocked into touch a yard from the line. Rome,. Powell, and Slazinger by a combined effort relieved, but only momentarily, for Hassell in quick succession conceded three minors. At this point Frank Turner was injured, and he retired from the field of play, Warrington now only playing fourteen men. Passing by the home backs raised a faint hope in the breasts of the Warrington enthusiasts, and then Berry, Nevins, and Holmes took the leather over, Hassell having the:hest of A maul. Evans made a bold bid for premier honours with an exact run, but it was left to Jolley to do the trick, for securing possession at the quarter flag, he was soon in his stride, and brushing his opponents aside, he ultimately scored after a somewhat clever run. Fair Turner took the place, his kick striking the post, half time then
I team.
