ODDFELLOWS' DINNER. The members of the Prosperity lodge No. 1,076, of the National Independent Order of Oddfellows, —.Warrington district,held their annual_ dinner at the Ram's Head Hotel, on Saturday night. A capital dinner, prepared Mr.l'. Forster, was partaken of by 24 of the members, and thoroughly enjoyed. After dinner a social evening was spent, songs be- ing given by several of the 'Ambers. SUTTON PRIMROSE Lnearn. A meeting and entertainment under the auspices of the Sutton Habitation of the Primrose League, was held in. the National Schools, Sutton, on Tues- day night, when about 500 were present. The pro- ceedings were under the presidency of Mr. W. Webster, jun., Ruling Councillor, and he was sup- ported on the platform by Mr. Robert Pierpoint,J.P. (Wairington), Mr. Joseph Robinson, Mr. B. Bevan, Mr. W. Robinson, Mr. J. Massey, &c. During the evening Mr. Pierpoint delivered an address, in which he advocated the principles of the league. An entertainment of a very interesting character followed.

div.head: ROSE KELLY FOR AMERICA.
div.p: ROSE KELLY FOR AMERICA.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. Timmis and Lieutenant-Colonel Gaskell, Rose Kelly, Caroline-street, was charged in custody with drunken- ness. Superintendent Noblett said the prisoner had been 80 times before the court previously. The prisoner, in answer to the charge, said she was going to America in about a month, and that would prevent her troubling the court again.—The Chairman : If we send you to gaol for 14 days, will you promise to keep sober until you go to America ?—Prisoner: Yes.—The prisoner was then committed to gaol for 14 days in default of paying a fine of 103. and costs.

div.head: ASTON UNITED DISTRICT SCHOOL. BOARD.
div.p: ASTON UNITED DISTRICT SCHOOL. BOARD.

At the meeting of the School Board for the Aston ' united district, held in Aston on Saturday morning, Mr. J. G. Best, chairman, an estimate was produced for the half-year ending Lady Day, 1891,from which it appeared that .£240 was required for the expenses of administra- tion and maintenance of school. After taking into ac- count school fees to be received, and balance at Michael- 1 mas, 1890, the sum of £ll7 was the amount of call re- quired, when it was resolved that contributions be signed upon the overseers of the townships for the fol- lowing amounts :—Aston, £37; Aston Grange, £7 • and Sutton, £46; total, £9O, being at the rate of lid. in the £on the rateable value of the district. Cheques to the amount of £33 7s. was signed for salaries, &c. due. EXIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canadn, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Union, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, "Examiner' Office, Bewsey-st., Warrington.—Advt. YOUNG THIEVES AT WIDNES.

On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, William McName (12), Ann St. West ; Joseph Edg,erley (11), Appleton-st., and James Broadhurst (11), Sutton-lane, were charged with stealing eight pigeons from a cote in Margaret-st„ the property ot John O'Brien. During Saturday night the cote was broken open and the pigeons stolen. On Sunday afternoon Broadhurst gave a boy named Walter Johnson five pigeons, and the latter hearing they had been stolen, handed them over to the poliee.—The pri- soners pleaded guilty and were each sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod.—Catherine Mark, 28. Water-street (14), and Sarah Glynn, 36. Water-st., (12), pleaded guilty to stealing Icwt. of coal from a wagon on the railway siding, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company, on the 2nd inst.— P.C. Robinson said on Thursday afternoon last he was on duty on the canal bank near Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s works, when he saw the two prisoners stealing the coal produced from a wagon in the siding.—The ' defendants were each fined ss. NOVEL BEGGING LETTER SWINDLE AT RI7NCORN. Yesterday, at the Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. James Handley and Dr. Steele, Mary Booth, an old woman, the wife of a scavanger, was charged with en- deavouring to collect charitable contributions by means of false and fraudulent pretences. Eliza Hollingworth, alias Hampson, was charged with counselling and pro- curing the commission of the offence. On the previous day Detective Woodrow found Mrs. Booth begging with a letter, of which the following is a copy :—" Run- corn, October 9th. John Pears have been ill for twelve months, and as died last night. My son in law. Please would you try to help us. His widow has five children. Mary Pears, Mayson-st." On the reverse side the following subscriptions were recorded :—Mrs. Holling,worth, is.; Mr. John Savage (draper), is. ; a friend, 3d. Wood row apprehended the woman, who then confessed that Mrs. Hollingworth had written the letter, and that they had arranged that she (Mrs. Booth) should go out and beg by its means, and then divide the spoil. Mrs. Hollingworth was then arrested. Evidence bearing out these facts having been given, the Bench sentenced each prisoner to two months' hard labour, both having been previously convicted for various offences. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. It W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adri. THE GIFFORD GUN_ AND ORDNANCE COMPANY

div.head: LIMITED.
div.p: LIMITED.

This Company—w,hose prospectus will be found on our front page—is formed, with a capital of X 250.000 in £1 shares, to acquire and work Mr Gifford's gun and ordnance patents. The liquified gas gun, invented by Mr. Prkul Gifford, is certainly a most remarkable weapon. It appears to be destined to create a new era in the manufacture and use of all classes of sporting guns and rifles, and also pistols and saloon arms. By it many. of the difficulties which hinder the adoption of magazine rifles are obviated. The guns, are capable according to calibre, of firing from 50 to 300 consecutive shots without re-charging. Among its other merits are a simplicity of mechanism, an entire absence of flame, smoke and dirt, it is practically noiseless and light, elegant, and inexpensive. The charge is not affected by water, and after tiring the exhausted reservoir can be replaced in a few seconds. The in- ventor of the gun—M. Paul Giffard—has accom- plished several notable things in the way of inven- tion. In 1853, in conjunction with his brother, he invented the well-known Giffard injector; he is the original inventor of the ref rigertor. used for the preservation of fresh meat, and in Paris the deli- very pf telegraphic letters is effected with extraor- dinary rapidity by Giffard's pneumatic tube sys- tem. It should be added that M. Paul Giffard will attend at the office of the Giffard Gun and Ord- nance Company (Copthall House, Copthall-avenue, London, E.G.), to-day (Saturday),between the hours of 2 p.m. and 4 p.m., to answer any questions con- nected with his invention, and to personally de- monstrate the gun. CRITCHLEY, High Class Tailor, Bold-st.Warrington.--Adat.

div.head: FATAL FALL AT COLLINS GREEN.
div.p: FATAL FALL AT COLLINS GREEN.

On Monday morning between six and seven o'clock, an old man about seventy years of age, named Thomas Dowd, was found dead in a stable on the Moss Hall Farm occupied by Mr. Gilroy, Collins Green. The deceased came to Collins Green about a fortnight ago, having just left the Workhouse, and obtained employment as a labourer, on the farm of Mr. Gilroy. On Sunday he complained of being unvvell, and in the afternoon Mr. Gilroy gave him a stimulant, repeating the dose at night. Dowd slept in aloft over the stable, and on Sunday night he locked the stable door, and after ascending to the loft, drew the ladder up after him. Next morning Mr: Gilroy found him lying in a corner of the stable huddled up, and dead, having evidently fallen through a bole in the loft. An inquest was held on the body at the Pear Tree Hotel, Collins Green, by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, on Thursday morning, when evidence bearing out the foregoing facts, was adduced, and the jury returned a verdict "Acci- dental death." Gls FITTINGs.--Garland, Gas Fitter, 51, Bridge-st., War- rington.—Advt.

div.head: MR. PETER SMITH AND HIS CUSTOMER. THE VALUE OF A BLACK EYE.
div.p: MR. PETER SMITH AND HIS CUSTOMER. THE VALUE OF A BLACK EYE.

Yesterday, at Widnes County Court, his Honour deputy Judge Goldthorpe,aud a common jury, were occupied for two hours hearing an action brought by Mr. William Sadler, grocer, Simms Cross, Widnes, I against Mr. Peter Smith, chemist of Widnes and Runcorn, to recover the sum of £lO damages for an assault. The defendant paid into court, with a denial of liability. Mr. J. W. Knowles, appeared for the plain- tiff and Dr. Commins, M.P. (instructed by Mr. Burton of Runcorn) defended. The facts as practically admitted by both sides are as follows. About five o'clock on the evening of the 13th August, the plaintiff went into Mr. Smith's shop in Victoria-road, Widnes, in order to make a purchase. The defendant, who was strange to the plaintiff, was standing on the cus- tomers' side of the counter. A dispute arose between the plaintiff and the shop boy as to the price of the article. The defendant told the boy to get the price list from the window, whereupon plaintiff said ‘• What have you got to do with it. Defendant replied that as he was proprietor of the shop, he ought to have some- thing to do with it. Further conversation ensured end- ing with plaintiff calling defendant a 'snotty pup." Detendant said if he called him that again he would knock him down, and plaintiff retorted by calling him a " mean snotty pup" and defendant struck him on the eye, causing him to fall to the floor.—The plaintiff in his evidence said he only called the defendant "snotty puppy" once and defendant immediately knocked him down.—Mr. H. W. Griffin, photographer, corroborated.— Dr. 0' Keeffe who had attended the plaintiff said he was suffering from an " ordinary black eye."—His Honour in summing up said there was no justification for the assault, but the plaintiff had used a very insulting expression, thus undoubtedly giving the defendant great provocation.—The jury after a brief consultation, returned a verdict that the sovereign paid into court was quite sufficient and his honour gave judgment for the defendant with costs,
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The 'Monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday night. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present—The Rev. Canon Wood, the Rev. Dr. Gasta'di, Dr. McDougall. Messrs. Howitt, Taylor, A. Salkeld, and G. Moss (clerk). THE LATE BOARD'S POLICY. On the reading of the minutes of the last meeting, the Chairman expressed his regret that he was not present at the last meeting to join in the congratulations on the success of the Board Schools, two of which had earned the excellent merit grant. He thought it only right that he should point out that these results were to be attri- buted to the work which was accomplished by the late Board. The late Board altered the character of the Greenway-road Board School, and provided a staff of teachers for that school, and also Mill Brow School, and the reports of the Government Inspector justified the policy adopted and the appointments made. The results were also creditable to the children themselves. The present Board had only to continue the same policy to make the schools a success in the future. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—WARM DISCUSSION. The School Attendance Committee presented their an nual report, which showed that 3,400 warning notices had been served by the visitors, previous year 3,200, in- crease 200 ; parents summoned to appear before the Committee, 637 ; preceding year 558, increase 79 ; pro- secutions before magistrates 87, preceding year 122 ; decrease 35 •, average number on the rolls 3,363, preced- ing year 3,330, increase 33 ; average attendance 2,708 ; preceding year 2,685 ; increase 23 ; percentage of atten- dance 80.5 ; preceding year 80.6, decrease 0.1. The cer- tified accommonation in the whole of the schools in the town is 500 more than the average attendance, but it worthy of remark that the whole of this surplus is in the schools on the north side of the canal, while those on the south side of the canal are full. All the children whom the Board has sent to industrial schools are now released, and the Board is not now making any contributions to these institutions.—Dr. Gastaldi in moving the adoption of the report said the Committee had not spared any work, or time, or pastime to obtain an increased attend- ance at all the sckools in the town, but so far as the average attendance was concerned they were at a stand- still; and he urged the Board to adopt the policy pur- sued by the late Board, and avail themselves of the resources which the law placed in their power.—The Chairman said the Committee had the control of the machinery for improving the attendance at school and it was to the Committee the Board would look for • improved results.—Mr. Salkeld seconded the adoption of the report.—ln answer to Mr. Howitt, the Clerk said in 1887 the per centage of attendance was 76 ; 1888, 81; 1889, 81 ; 1890, 81.—Mr. Hewitt said in Widnes,w here the number of convictions before the magistrates were very ' much more numerous than in Runcorn,there was no better attendance. He contended that the figures presented by Dr. Gastaldi proved that the attendance now was better than the attendance obtained by the preceding Board. He objected to send parents before the magistrates to be made criminals of,unless all other means of kindness and persuation had failed. It was the duty of the members to see that the children were educated and if the parents had not a proper interest in the welfare of the children, the members should try personally to persuade parents to send their children regularly to school.—Mr. Taylor said Dr. Gastaldi's statement was practically a vote of censure upon the members of the Committee. He characterised the manner in which parents were sent before the magistrates by the late Board as cruelty, and said this year the number had been reduced from 122 to 87, and it would not be his fault if next year this figure was not -very much less. If they could not obtain their object without such an abominable system, they would not gain it with that system, and he was sorry to hear Dr. Gastaldri encourage the members to adopt any such means. Dr. Gastaldi referred to the previous Board as much as to say that the present Board had not done its duty, and ii that were so Dr. Gastaldi as Chairman was greatly responsible—Mr. Salkeld said from his own ex- perience and observations he knew that Dr. Gastaldi had done his utmost both in his own flock and everyone elses to bring the childrento school by kindness and per- suasion.—Canon Wood said Mr. Jordan wished him to state that the attendance had been worse at his school lately owing, he believed to a want of firmness on the part of the School Board, and if this relaxity were continued the result would become worse. He depreciated the importation of motives in what was purely a matter of opinion on policy, and he was sure that Mr. Taylor, on consideration would feel that he had made a mistake.—Mr. Howitt asked wherein had Mr. Taylor imputed motives.—Canon Wood replied in the use of the word cruelty.—Dr. MacDougall commenced to speak on the subject when Mr. Howitt rose to a point of order. He said a member in addressing the chair ought to pay due deference by standing up.—Dr. MacDougall : I do not take you as an authority on manners. It is absolutely nonsense and I decline to discuss the question I urther.Dr. Grastaldi, in replying to a discussion, said as persuasion and kindness and personal influence, he had tried it to the fullest extent and he was disgusted with the results; and he could not carry it on any further. He contended that too much sympathy and kindness made the parents repeat the same offence. As Chairman of the Committee he had exhausted all his kindness and patience. When they found that the same people were always brought before the Committee for neglect, it seemed to him time to resort to the utmost power the law gave the Board.—The motions were passed. SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE. The School Management Commit tee recommended that the salary of Miss Kennan, head teacher at Mill Brow Infants School be advanced to £B5 per annum. Recommended that the resignation of Miss Price, assist- ant teacher at Greenway-road Girls School, be accepted, and that a successor be advertised for. The Clerk drew the attention dl the Committee to the report of the Committee of Council on education in which School

Boards and Voluntary Schools were impressed with the necessity of teaching girls some practical instruction in cookery, and the Committee recommended the subject to the consideration of the Board. The minutes were adopted and the question of cooking was deferred. _

THE NIGHT CLASSES. Mr. • Pritchard reported to the School Management Committee that he had attended the opening of the even- ing school at Greenway-road Boys' School ; when 37` boys and young men presented themselves as pupils ; 28 of these wished to learn the elementary subjects and mathe- matics, and at least 20 were anxious for shorthand. It was recommended that the fees per week be as follows: —Standard subjects, 4d. ; shorthand in addition, 2d. ; shorthand alone, 4d.—The Clerk remarked that there was now between 70 and 80 pupils at the night classes, which he thought would be a great success, and much appreciaten by the youths of the town.

div.head: -A YEAR'S FINANCE.
div.p: -A YEAR'S FINANCE.

The Clerk presented a financial statement for the year ended the 29th September, 1890. The receipts were as follows :-Balance in hand on Sept. 29th, 1889, £l9B 15s. 7d. ; grants from education department, £490 13s. Bd. ; payment by the rating authorities, £950 ; school fees, £315 us. sd. ; books and other articles sold to children, £ll Os. 10d. ; rent for schoolroom, £5 ; loan of ballot boxes, 10s. ; total, £1,971 us. 4d.-Theexpen- diture was as follows :-Election expenses, £95 10s. 3d. ; salaries of officers of the Board, £284 18s. 4d. ; legal and other expenses of administration, £73 Bs. 2d. ; salaries of teachers, £697 4s. 3d. ; books, apparatus, and stationary, £52 16s. 4d.; fuel, light, cleaning, and repairs, £ll4 16s. lid ; rents, rates, and taxes, £7 Bs. Bd. ; other ex- penses of maintenance, £8 is. 7d.; contributions to in- dustrial schools, £23 13s. 9d. ; furnishing school build- ings £l4 17s. 6d.; repayment of principal of loans. £147 Os. id. ; interest on loans, £176 17s. 6d. ; total, £1,696 6s. 4d. ; leaving a balance in hand of £275 ss. The out standing liabilities of the Board amounted to £4,728 is. Bd.-The statement was approved, and the Clerk suggested that a precept for £5OO should be served upon the overseers.-This proposal was agreed to.

A CHEMISTRY CLASS FORMED. Mr. Poole, secretary to the Science and Art School,wrote asking that Mr. J. Knowles should be permitted to have the use of a room at the Greenway-road school, for the purpose of teaching technicologieal chemistry (alkali manufacture) under the City and Guilds of London In- stitute, on the same terms as the room was allowed to Mr. Cook. After some discussion, the application was granted on the motion of Mr. Salkeld, seconded by Mr. Howett. Mr. Salkeld observed that such a class was greatly needed for the neighbourhood. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery, on Wednesday. Mr. S. Taylor presided and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. R. Morris, E. Imison, T. Handley, H. Coleburn, W. Mellor, W. Whittaker and W. F. Salkeld (clerk.) The Secretary reported that during the six months ended September 25th, there were 207 interments ; same period last year 192 ; increase 15. The fees received during the same period amounted to £207 2s. Bd. ; last year £l7O 15s. ; increase £36 7s. Bd.—On the recommenda- tion of the Finance Committee, accounts amounting to £23s. 7d., and interest amounting to £23 Bs. were passed for payment.—The Chairman said the question as to whether the Board should purchase any more land for cemetery purposes. had been discussed at previous meet- ings, and adjourned to that occasions for a decision. A month ago the Secretary reported that the Board had sufficient land to meet the requirements of the town for 90 years.—Mr. Handley said he expected they would have a new mode of disposing of bodies by that time, and he thought the Board need not bother about more land.—Mr. Whittaker: lam inclined to think the same. —Dr. Gastaldi said he expressed a similar opinion to Mr. Handley at a previous meeting, and he considered the question of purchasing more land irrelevant to the pre- sent time.—On the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Dr. Gastaldi, it was resolved that no land be purchased at present.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTRORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided. Present—Messrs. J. Stokes, J.Baguley, Heywood, P. Hall, J. Bate, Bretherton, H. Linaker (clerk), and H. G. Linaker (deputy-clerk).
THE POLLUTION OF ICECKWICK BROOK.

Inspector Farrington said Colonel Ducat, the Local Government Board Inspector' wished him to take a sample of water from Preston Brook before it joined the Keckwick Brook, and received the stuff that came from the tanyard. The Inspector also wished to be furnished with a copy of the analysis as soon as possible.—The re- quisite instructions were given.

- FEVER OUTBREAKS. Dr. Adams (medical officer), reported that there was one case of diptheria at Walton, the disease having arisen through drinking water from a well on the pre- mises, which on analysis proved to be unfit for domestic purposes, and the use of the well has been discontinued. Water from Warrington Waterworks was now supplied to the house. A case of diptheria had also occurred at London Bridge. A mild case of the same disease had taken place at Helsby, but the source of the disease was not determined. A case of typhoid fever had occurred at Alvanley, the cause of the disease being a combina- tion of insanitary conditions. A case of the same disease had also occurred at Frodsham Bridge. The cause of the disease was obscure. Typhoid fever had also occurred at three houses in Overton, Frodsham Lordship. The 1 Medical Officer suggested that the water supply should be at once analysed. A mild case of diptheria had oc- curred at Sutton Weaver. There were no insanitary conditions discovered.—The usual preventative order had been issued.
NEW HOUSES. Certificates of occupation were granted to four houses at Lower Walton, belonging to Mr. Frederick Monks.
RUNCORN TONIC SAL FA CONCERTS.

The Runcorn Tonic Sal Fa Choir commenced their sixth season on Monday evening, when a miscel- laneous concert was given in the Public Hall, and that their efforts to spread a knowledge of music are appreciated, was shown by the audience of con- siderable proportions which assembled. Mr. Halford, the conductor, had arranged an attractive programme, and the following principals were engaged :—Miss Ada Lee (soprano), Mr. J. W. Maltby (bass), of Manchester, Miss Nunn, L.R.A.M. (solo pianoforte),and Miss Gordon Nunn (solo violin). The concert commenced with the part song "Empire Flag," in which the choir displayed the qualities now associated with their work—precision, expression, and tunefulness. The madrigal "Hard by a fountain," was a most enjoyable number, and Ben Jonson's "See the chariot at hand" was very brightly rendered. In the second part the choir sang "The fisherman's bride," and "On the sea," with much taste, and the audience did not fail to announce their approval. Mr. Maltby was suffering from a throat affection, and although he sang " The night watch,' and "So Sir Page" in the first part of the entertainment he did not fulfil his engagement in the second Dart, and much regret was expressed and disappointment felt. Miss Ada Lee, who is the possessor of a bright and clear soprano voice, contributed" The Glen Maiden," "Some day," On the banks of Allan Water," and " Tell me my heart," in each of which she displayed vocid powers of no mean order. She was enthusiastically encored for her vocalisation of the last named song. A most enjoyable feature of the concert was the instrumental music, the audience being charmed and delighted by the brilliant performances of the Misses Nunn on the piano and violin; and both ladies had to respond to encores. Miss Gordon Nunn brought the company to a high pitch of enthusiasm by her manipulation of the violin, her performances evidencing all the ability and skill of a master hand. Mr. Halford weilded the conductor's baton with his usual efficiency, and Mrs. W. B. Kay ably officiated as accom- panist.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon. Major J. W. Wareing, presided, and there were also present the Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. F. Stapleton Bretherton, J.P., Marsh, Middlehurst, Fisher, Johnson, Tyrer, Lowe, Ranson, Davies, Kenwright, Jos. Birchen, Mercer, Buckley, Graves, Leatherbarrow, Goldworth, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). THE WORKHOUSE INnitAnts.—The Master of the Work- house reported there were 491 inmates of the house this week, 479 last week, 499 in the corresponding period last year; 72 vagrants had been relieved against 51 last year. He also acknowlAged the receipt of a hamper of apples from Roby Church harvest thanksgiving service, and a. parcel of papers from the Prescot Cocoa Rooms. ASSISTANT OVERSEERS' SALARIES.—OR the recommenda- tion of the Finance Committee, it was resolved that the salaries of Messrs. John Kitchen and H. A. Twist, assist- ant-overseers, be £l6O each for twelve months from the 25th March last. NEW APPOINTMENTS.—The Local Government Board wrote that they had no objection to the appointment of Milicent Thorpe, as nurse at the Workhouse at a salary of £3O per annum.—Mr. Marsh gave notice that at the next meeting he should move the re-appointment of Mr. R. G. Waterman as School Attendance and Inquiry Officer for the Woolton district, at a salary of £130. Mr. Davies gave notice that at the next meetinghe should move the appointment of an assistant relieving officer for the Widnes district at a salary of £2O per annum. THE CHARGE OF DESERTION AGAINST AN EX-TOWN COUNCILLOR.—The Clerk read a letter from Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. Helens, stating that the period in which Mr. W. J. Kirkham had been allowed to pay the money owing to the Guardians for the maintenance of his chidren had expired, and as Mr. Kirkham had not been able to obtain work, he wished for another month's grace.—The matter was left in the hands of the Clerk. THE POOR LAW CONFERENCE.—Mr. Middlehurst re ported on the proceedings at the recent Poor Law Con- ference, and a vote of thanks was tendered to him. This was the principal business.

div.head: GUARDS IN BERMUDA.
div.p: THE GUARDS IN BERMUDA.

REPORTED SERIOUS FEVER OUTBREAK. NEW YORE, THllESDAY.—Despatches received at Hali- fax from Bermuda report that a serious outbreak of enteric fever has occurred in the British garrison there. It is stated that the disease is making havoc with the Grenadiers recently sent there, and that many of the men are dying.
TRAGEDIES AT NOTTINGHAM FAIR

The pleasure fair at Nottingham closed on Saturday in a tragic manner. A woman named Taylor, a shooting glilery proprietress, dropped dead while talking to some friends. Edward Holmes, a gingerbread dealer of City- road, London, went ts rest in a van shortly after mid- night. About five on Sunday morning the van was seen on fire, and before the llamas could be extinguished Holmes was burned to death.

DEATH OF MR SUPERINTENDENT WEIR. The death of Mr. Superintendent Weir for five years head of the Warrington County Police Divi- sions, whose headquarters were at Leigh, took place about three o'clock on Sunday morning. It was a most unexpected and melancholy occurrence, for Mr. Weir seemed to enjoy robust health until quite recently. His energies were taxed to the uttermost in unravelling the mystery that for a long time sur- rounded the murder of a young pawnbroker's assist- ant named Walter Davies, a native of Widnes at Atherton, in July last year, and he was largelyin- strumental in securing the conviction of Williana Chadwick, who at length suffered the extreme penalty of ' the law at Kirkdale. Scarcely had the last of the Atherton murder been heard of than Mr. Weir had to take in band_ the Ship Canal shooting ease at Risley. The accused likewise in this case eluded the vigilance of the police • for a month or two, but was ultimately apprehended. Mr. Weir left off duty on the 113th ult. On Wednesday last he went to Southport with Mra. Weir, being obliged ' to return on Friday, when he fell twice at Wigan Station. Paralysis of the brain set in on Saturday. He was under the care of Dr. King, of Leigh, and Dr. Dreschfield, of Manchester, was called in on Saturday afternoon, and he held out no hope•of recovery, a blood vessel having burst in the head and the left side was paralyzed. Mr. Weir had been 29 years in the constabu- lary, and previous to coming to this country he was in the Royal Irish force. He was born in the North of Ireland; As inspector of police he was stationed at Burnley, then he was appointed superintendent of the Wigan county division, whence he was transferred to Leigh as successor to Superintendent Jackson, who resigned on a pension. He was a zealous and efficient officer, and his death in the prime of life (54) is a loss to the force, and it will be regretted by the public in the districts of Leigh, Newton-le-Willows, Earlestown, and Warrington, and by the police under his charge. De- ceased, who had made arrangements to visit America, and to sail next Saturday, leaves a widow, a son, and three daughters. In politics he was a Conservative, and he was also a Churchman and a Freemason. MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE.

Before commencing the business at the Leigh Police Court, on Monday, the Chairman (Mr. A. Burrows) referred on behalf of the magistrates to the death of Superintendent Weir. He said Mr. Weir was a most efficient and able officer, and was universally esteemed by everyone with whom he came in contact. The police force would suffer greatly by his loss, and the magis- trates desired him to express their deep sympathy with the widow and family of the deceased. They contended that Mr. Weir had been a victim to overwork; in fact, by the extension of his division a great amount ef labour had devolved upon him. On behalf of the officials of the Court Mr. W. E. Marsh, magistrates' clerk, regretted the loss they had sustained. Mr. Weir had the Atherton murder case under his charge, and it was mainly due to his efforts that the murderer was brought to the bar of justice. Mr. Weir had also under his care the Cadishead murder .case... These. two

cases, combined with his ordinary work in the division, which was by no means light, had produced traces of overwork, which were apparent to those with whom he came in contact during the last few months. Notwith- standing the work he had to do, Mr. Weir had performed it to the best of his ability and to the satisfaction of all concerned. Mr. F. 13. Taylor also testified, on behalf of the solici- tors, to the loss they had sustained. On behalf of the family of the late superintendent, Inspector Hodgson thanked the magistrates, the clerk, and the solicitors for their sympathetic remarks. THE FUNERAL

The funeral of the deceased gentleman took place at Burnley, on Wednesday morning. Shortly after ten o'clock a procession was formed at the deceased's resid- ence, which consisted of a number of sergeants, con- stables, Freemasons, and mourners, who followed the remains of the deceased to the Leigh and Bedford Rail- way Station (London and North-western), where it was conveyed by train en route for Burnley, where the inter- ment took place.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and there were also present, Aldermen Holmes, Davies. Harrison, Sutton, Chandley ; Councillors Platt. H. Robertsi Blackhurst, Pierpoint, Fleming, Cannell, Shaw Green, Muir, Ashton, Voisey, Hepherd, Greene% Heaton, Garner, Hatchinson, R. T. Fairclough, Per- cival, Flood Tinsley, Taylor; Messrs. 3, L. Whittle (town clerk), Longdin (borough engineer), and Chorley (borough treasurer). PUBLIC HEALTH AND DISEASE PREVENTION. On the motion of the blazon it was decided that parts 2,3, 4, and 5 of the Public Health Acts Amendment Act, 1890, and all the sections of the Infectious Diseases Pre- vention Act, 1890, should come into operation in the borough on the 19th ot November. THE RESIGNATION OP COUNCILLOR MONKS.—THE PINE NOT PAID. The MATOH said he had received the following letter from Councillor Monks :--" Dear Mr. Mayor,—For some time I have felt desirous of retiring from the Town Council and now that November is near I shall be obliged if you will place my resignation before the Council so that no additional trouble or expense would be incurred in November in filling my place.—Yours faithfully, F. Motixs."—He (the Mayon) might say that as Councillor Monks had not paid his fine of Ls. theTovrn Clerk advised him that they could not accept that resignation. It therefore remained as it was. THE TREATMENT OF A POLICE SERGEANT. A HARD CASE. The MAYOR moved the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Committee, and Alderman WRIGHT seconded. Councillor ROBERTS said he should like permission to ask a question ;he did not wish to enter into any dis- cussion. Was it a fact that the Watch Committee were desirous of re-funding to ex-Police Sergeant Shaw the amount of money which he had contributed to the sup- erannuation fund, that such desire of the Committee had been intimated to the Chief Constable, that the Com- mittee cannot act in the matter without a recommenda- tion to that effect from the Chief Constable, that the Chief Constable had refused to make such recommenda- tion, and if the Watch Committee were acquainted with the reasons of the Chief Constable for so refusing. The MAYOR said that, in answer to Councillor Roberts he should like to say that the Watch Committee had the case of the superannuation fund before them, and a majority—he thought almost every member of the Watch Committee would have been pleased to have given Sergeant Shaw- the whole of the money that he had paid toward the fund, but it appeared that the Watch Committee had no power whatever to do that unless the Chief Constable would recommend it, and that Mr. Hunt blankly refused to do. Of ceurse all the Watch Committee could then do was to beat a graceful retreat and leave it. Councillor ROBERTS said that was the position he understood th 3 Watch Committee to be in. Ha should consider whether ornot to move a resolution at the next Council meeting on the subject. Alderman HARRISON said he should like to supplement what the Mayor had said. Mr. Hunt hardly put it quite so strongly as the Mayor did. He (Alderman Harrison) would not venture to say that the whole of !the members of the Watch Committee would really point blank give to the police officer the amount suggested. He would say that there was a favourable inclination on the part of the members of the Watch Committee to do so, but they did not by any means commit themselves to it. Mr. Hunt said that, having regard to certain cir- cumstances which had taken place, he should be very glad if he could conscientiously recommend the Watch Committee to do it, but he saw there was a difficulty in the way—he said his conscience would not permit it. (A laugh.) If his conscience would not permit him to do so they could do nothing but respect his scruples. Councillor Piarr saidthat, as a member of the Watch Committee, he very much regretted the decision Mr. Hunt had come to in that matter. He thought that all along P.S. Shaw had not had the consideration he was entitled to. That was his (Councillor Platt's) private opinion, and though it might not coincide with the opin- ion of the majority of the Watch Committee, he felt bound to express it. He was the person who proposed at the Watch Committee that the money should be re- funded ex-P.S. Shaw, and every member of the Com- mittee then present was perfectly willing. (Hear, hear.) • The minutes of the Watch Committee were then adopted. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE.— A SANKEY-ST. SHOP. This Committee recommended that the plans of the following buildings, &e., be approved :—Six houses in Forster-st.. for Mr. Joseph Grounds; greenhouse in yard, at rear of 79, Rostock-st., for Mr. A. Rawlinson ; green- house in yard, at rear of 92, Bostock-st., for Mr. Joseph Heesom ; four houses in Marsh House-lane, for Mr. Alfred Worrall ; additions to house. No. 8, Tanner's-lane, for Mr. J. P. Edelsten •, additions to cottage at Messrs.. Tinsley's Tannery, Mersey-st. Also, that the following report of the Lighting Sub-Committee be approved and adopted :—Thyrine=st. : Remove pillar lamp, opposite No. 25, to corner of curb, next passage. Passage to Museum-st. : Fix new bracket lamps on wall of Mr. Fletcher's works, mid-way between Museum-st. and Thynne-st. Museum-st. : Remove pillar lamp on north side to within a yard of corner of passage to Thynne-st., and insert new pillar lamp on south side, where marked 'X, 32 yards west of Arpley-st. Elizabeth-st. : Fix new bracket lamp on corner of house No. 50. Cartwright-st. : Fix new pillar lamp opposite No. 50, fix new pillar lamp between Nos. 61 and 63. Lodge-lane: Fix four new I pillar lamps, one opposite west gate of the late Mr. J. Pierpoint's house, and three others, Wenly spaced, between last named and lamp under railway bridge. Arpley : One new pillar lamp on south side of iron rail- way bridge, leading to cricket field. Councillor PLATT moved and Alderman WEIGHT seconded the conformation of the minutes of the Com- mittee. Councillor FLE3fING asked if it was not possible for the Corporation to have the shop in Sankey-st. (near Legh-st.) set back. If the Corporation had power to refuse to pass the plans it might have been done. Councillor Pim, said the Committee were desirous to have the shop set back but they found they were absolutely powerless in the matter. The premises had not been interfered with to an extent that would allow the Committee to insist upon its being set back. The minutes were then agreed to.

SANITARY COMMITTEE.—THE CHAIRMAN'S HOLI- DAY.—COMPLAINTS ABOUT THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS. This Committee recommended as follows :—That the tender of Mr. John Chorley to supply two tons of hoop iron at £7 103. per ton be accepted; that the tender of William Chester and George Fern to supply 20 dozen scavengers' brooms at 19s. per dozen; 10 sets of machine brushes at 40s. 6d. ; and 3 dozen spoke brushes at 16s. 9d. per dozen, each be accepted; that the tender of Messrs. Marshall, Sons and Co., Limited, to supply a 10 H.P. Engine for Longford Depot at £165 delivered, be accepted. Alderman SUTTON moved the confirmation of the minutes. He said Alderman Burgess, the Chairman of the Committee, was taking the benafit of some relaxa- tion which it was deemed advisable he should enjoy from the arduos duties which the sanitary department and other important matters had, during the last few years, entailed upon him. He was sure that they all hoped that Alderman Burgess would, on the completion of his holi- days, return to his duties fully invigorated and able, in the interests of the borough, to resume the active part he had always taken in the work of the Corporation with the same energy and enthusiasm that had marked his con- duct through the long number of years he had been a member of that Corporation. Alderman Wanarr seconded. Councillor PLATT wished the Committee would again take into their consideration the condition of the inter- cepting depot at Lythgoes-lane. After taking particular notice of it for some months, he was strongly of opinion that the money spent there in trying to obviate the smell was entirely wasted. Councillor Mum suggested that the Council should take the matter of these depots into serious consideration, and if anything could be done it should be done at once. Councillor GREENALL agreed with Councillor Muir. , No steps had been taken be cause the Chairman of the Committee would not answer questions or give inform- ation to the Council. He (Councillor Greenall) had sent a letter to the Committee and asking that it should be acknowledged, but it had not been acknowledged and he believed it had been ignored altogether. Councillor Romurrs thought it was rather ungenerous to attack the Chairman personally in his absence. Councillor Greenall knew perfectly well that Alderman Burgess was weight enough for him if he had been there and half-a-dozen besides. Alderman CHANDLRY (interrupting) said he thought there were extremely improper remarks to make. The MAYOR: I think Councillor Greenall said he sent a letter to the Committee. Councillor ROBERTS replied that when Councillor Greenall said that the Chairman of the Committee would not give information to the members of that Council. The Chairman not being there for the first time for many years it was unfair to make an attack upon him in his absence, and as a member of that Council and a personal friend he (Councillor Roberts) was not going to be the one to listen to a personal attack without rebutting it. The letter which Councillor Greenall referred to had been under discussion and the Town Clerk was requested to acknowledge it in the usual way. As to going into the details of the matter referred to it was not considered to be in the interest of the Corporation to do so. Let it be thoroughly understood that the Chairman was not the Committee and the Committee was not the Chairman. They were all responsible for what was done, but as long as they had a Chairman like the one they had he was not going to sitthere and hear him abused without saying something in his defence. Councillor VOISET said there had been complaints about the depots several times but the complaints had never taken any definite shape. If there was any mem- ber of the Council who was still of opinion there was something to put right he should come with a full state-

div.p: _ THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 11, 1890.

ment of his grievances. They did not want any more general statements but the precise nature of the charges. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH said he lived as near the Howley depot as any member of the Council, and for the last twelve months he had never smelt it. He also spoke in favour of precise statements as to when the nuisance existed and then there would be something to act upon.; • Alderman Surrox said if it was supposed the Commit- tee were not taking any interest in the complaints made as to the depots it was a great mistake. The Committee ; were continually considering complaints and doing all in their power to abate any nuisance. They had referred ; the question to the medical officer and instructed him to report upon it, and he said as a member of the Commit- tee that if he found there was a nuisance existing of the alarming description which was represented he should be one of the very first to say "Let those depots be done away with." (Hear, hear.) Councillor PLATT asked what proof was required. An hour previously the depot was smelling at a distance of 200 yards. He did not know whether his word was worth anything or not, but by the last answer he got from the Committee when he made a complaint it was not worth anything. He did not know what they were to act upon except the word and those who knew. The minutes were then adopted.
powers with regard to the construction of new baths 1' He merely put the question to obtain information, and did not _wish to harass the Committee.
The MAYOR: The Act is not in force until the 30th of this month; it will be brought before the Committee at the earliest oppgrtunity.

Alderman SUTTON remarked that he should like to say a word with reference to the gardens. He dared say that they had noticed some newspaper comments de- nouncing the parks and gardens as being about the worst in existence. He did not think that the writer was in slightest degree justified in slandering the park to the extent that had been done. Many friends who had visited Warrington, had expressed to him on many occa- sions the pleasure that they had derived in having a walk round the gardens, and had stated that they had been in many parks and gardens in other towns, but had not seen any that were so well kept and so nice as they were in Warrington. They could not have large trees, because the noxious vapours destroyed them, but he thought they might be justly proud of the park, and the Committee—he was a member—(laughter)—and of everyone connected with it. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then confirmed.
Alderman Smrrox : It is one of the most ridiculous motions ever produced in this Council. Councillor FLOOD: It does not suit you, Alderman Sutton. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTER.
div.p: PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTER.

The minutes of this Committee contained the follow- ing resolutions :—That the tender of Mr. Simeon Hough for the forming and paving of part of St. Mary's-st., at £23 Is. 9d., be accepted ' • that the tender of Mr. William Bennett to supply 50,000 tiles at 775. ed. per 1,000; and the tender of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway to supply 50,000 tiles at 775. ed. per 1,000, be accepted; that the sewer in Cartwright-st. be continued to the nearest end of new cottages belonging to Mr. Wallington. Aderman Dimas proposed, and Councillor TAYLOR seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. • The motion was adopted. . SCHOOL ATTIINDANCE COMMITTEE.

Report of the Inspector to the School Attendance Com- mittee stated, that 61 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 53 cases for 113 children ; that 54 cases had been taken before the Magistrates and fines inflicted in 48 cases; 2 boys sent to the ship "Clio ;" 1 ordered to be flogged; 1 ordered to the workhouse, and 2 warrants ordered. 46 cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with. The average attendance at the Public Elementary Schools during the month of August waS 7,99l,correspond- ing period last year 7,72 l—increase 270. The Committee had resolved, that each of the Inspectors be provided with a mackintosh and a pair of leggings. ,

Councillor FLEMING proposed virie -adoption of the minutes of this Committee. The Council would see, he said, a small item that they intended to give the Inspec- tors a macintosh and a pair of leggings. He did not think that the Council would object to that. In other towns the Inspectors were provided with uniforms.

The minutes were confirmed. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE. The following was contained in the minutes of this Committee :—Return for the month of August: Visitors to the Museum 2,954, increase 8 per cent, compared with _August, 1889 ; books issued in reading room 1,387, de- crease 4 per cent, compared with August, 1889; books issued in lending department 2,128, decrease 6 per cent. compared with August, 1889 ; report of the following gifts, for which the thanks of the Committee were or- dered to be sent to the donors :—A Golden Pheasant, from the Town Hall Committee; "Scientific spirit of the age," by Miss F. P. Cobbe, from the author ; "Uni- versity Correspondence College Guides," 4 vols., from the publishers; " Heyrich and Hollinworth," by C. W. Sutton, from the author: "Liverpool Geological Asso- ciation," vol. 9. from the Association; "Journal of the Iron and Steel Institute," part 1., 1890, from the Insti- tute • catalogue of Birds, catalogue of Fossil Reptilia, Guide to Geology, 6 vols., from the Trustees of the British Museum. Minute, that a letter had been re- ceived from the Secretary of the National Gallery, say- ing that the Trustees consented to lend a collection of Turner's drawings and sketches for a period of twelve months, on the following conditions, viz. :-1. Incur- rance against fire for £2,000. 2. Protection against damp and exposure to the sun's rays. '3. No gas to be used in the room. 4. The drawings to be conveyed from the National Gallery to the Warrington Museum, and returned in the custody of some officer of the Museum, and at the cost of the latter institution. Re- solution, that the loan be accepted, and that the Curator be directed to fetch and return the collection in accor- danee with the conditions. Resolution, that Mr. Chorley be instructed, to insure the Turner drawings for a year from the 22nd September' in the Commercial Union In- surance Co., for £2,000. Resolution, that the insurance policy of the contents of the Museum be altered, so that the sum of £3,000, which is now stated to be upon loans, may cover either loans or additions to the property on the Corporation. and that the following be inserted, viz.: Landscape by Whaite, £5OO, and marble figure of Rachel, by Wood, £2OO. Resolution, that the old Latchford Stocks be lent to the School of Art for a month. Minute. that a letter had been received from the Science and Art Department saying that the applica- tion of this Committee for aid towards the purchase of photographs and specimens amounting to £75 15s. 6d., was approved, and that a grant of 50 per cent, of the cost would be made. Resolution, that Mr. Monks be allowed the use of the Art Gallery and other rooms for a conversazione upon, the Usual terms. • Councillor fl. ROBERTS, in proposing that the minutes be confirmed, explained that the minute having refe- rence to the proposed purchase of photographs and specimens, was a letter in answer to an application that had been made prior to the discussion in the Council on the question. They did not now propose to spend the money on photographs. Alderman DATIES seconded the prDposal. COURCHIOT MUIR suggested that more carpeting might be laid on the boarding at the Museum, as at present the noise made was a disturbance to readers. The minutes were then passed. CEMETERY COAMITTEB. From the report of the Registrar to the Cemetery Com- mittee it appeared that the interments for the past four weeks were :—Adults. 35; minors, 48 ; stillborn and pre- mature, 4. And for the corresponding period last year: —Adults, 25; minors, 64; stillborn and premature, 7. The receipts for the past four weeks were £6O 175: 3d., and for the corresponding period last year 284154.9 d., The minutes were confirmed on the' proposition of of Alderman HARRISON, seconded by Councillor Havron. TOWN HALL, PARK AND BATHS COMMITTER. - . _ .

From the report' Of .the Bath-keeper to the Committee it appeared that the income from the baths during the past four weeks was £23 18s. 2d• and for the correspond- ing period last year £lB ss. (a. The Committee had passed the following resolutions :—.-That the sum of £8 be voted for the purchase of hyacinths and bulbs; and that the thanks of the Committee be given to Miss Wallington, of Latchford, for the gift of six birds for the aviary. The MAYOR proposed, and Councillor BOLTON seconded, the confirmation of the report. ' Councillor H. ROBERTS asked for information as to how soon it was intended to proceed for the borrowing

div.head: MARKETS COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE MARKETS COMMITTEE.

The Markets Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. J. S. Garland to supply patent sand blast appara- tus at £l6, be accepted. The total income of the Com- mittee from all sources was £304 4s. 3d. The report was adopted on the motion of Councillor GREENALL, seconded byCouncillor liteminonsx.

div.head: TEN GAS ANALYSES.
div.p: TEN GAS ANALYSES.

The Gas Committee recommended that the public analyst be requested to test and report monthly to the General Purposes Committee upon the illuminating power of the gas. The average illuminating power of the gas during the past six weeks was equal to 18.51 candles, at both works. Alderman FIOLMES proposed and Alderman DATIES seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of this Com- mittee. Alderman Scrrox said that he thought the gas con- sumers had a perfect right to complain, as they did, and had done for a long time, of the fearfully bad quality of the gas. It was an indisputable fact that the light to be obtained from three or four burners in an ordinary apartment was not equal on many occasions to that of a small oil lamp. Then everybody must have witnessed for themselves the extremely faint light we had in our shops and streets.—(A voice : We have it here.) As the complaints were loud and numerous, he did think that the Committee should try to improve the quality of the gas. Councillor CANNELL complained of the disgraceful state of some of the streets after the laving of the gas pipes. Alderman WRIGHT replied that an understanding had been come to between the Gas and the Paving and Sew. Committee by which the latter Committee would look after the matter.

Alderman Hotoons, replying on the discussion, said that he could not accept the statement that the quality of gas was bad, although the pressure hod been consider- ably reduced, and the light had not been so good as be- fore. When they investigated complaints they usually found that the burners at the houses were not sufficient, and that if there were proper appliances there would be no complaint to make. Mr. Haddock informed him that he generally found that to be the case. The minutes were then confirmed.

LOCAL FIRES. From the report of the Superintendent to the Fire Engine Committee it appeared that the following fires had occurred :—On the 11th instant, at premises occupied by Mr. W. W. Dobson, Cabinet Maker, Buttermarket-st. ; On the 18th instant, at premises occupied by Mr. J. J. Brooks, Nursery Farm, Rixton ; On the 20th instant at the premises occupied bv Mr. Thomas Hewitt, Fir Tree Farm, Stretton ; On the 22nd instant at premises occupied by Mrs. B. Crosby, Marsh End Farm, Cuerdley. It was resolved that the Borough Treasurer be instructed to forward the following accounts for payment :—Mr. W. W. Dobson, £3 9s. 5d.; Mr. J. J. Brooks, £lB Os. 10d. ; Mr. Thomas Hewitt, £l4 us. 4d. ; Mrs. B. Crosby, £l7 is. 9d. Approved on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor PERCIVA.L.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTER.-THE NEW WARDS. At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee, it was resolved that the plan of the delimitation of the borough into nine wards now submitted by the Town Clerk be approved. At a meeting held on the 22nd September it was resolved that the following names be given to the new wards of the borough :-1, Town Hall Ward; 2, Whitecross Ward; 3, Bewsev Ward; 4, Orford Ward; 5, St. John's Ward; 6, Fairs2ld Ward; 7, Howley Ward; 8, St. Austin's Ward; 9, Latchford Ward.
The MAYOR proposed and Alderman HormEs seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of this Committee.

Councillor PLATT said that he thought the Committee had wasted money in advertising in two papers, in re- gard to the Commissioners award, whereas " the most influential " paper inserted the matter as one of public interest, and as news. Why should it be paid for, when the public could get to know without it being paid for? The MAYOU : I can only tell you that the Act requires that it shall he advertised in one or more papers. The minutes were adopted. COUNCILLOR FLOOD'S MOTION. A TORY STAMPEDE.

Councillor noon had given notice of his intention to propose the following motion :--" Any person or firm tendering for a contract with- the Council shall be required to make a declaration that they may pay such rates of wages and assure such hours of labour as are generally accepted as fair in the trade, and in the etent of any charges to the contrary being established against them their tenders shall not be accepted." When in the order of business the proper time for the motion to be introduced was reached, however, a number of the Con- servative members rose from their seats and left the Council Chamber. . Alderman Sul-mg : I should like to ask whether the question embodied in that resolution that he has given notice of is one that this Council can deal with. I think we should have that question settled. Councillor FLOOD: There is not a quorum. Alderman SUTTON: I want to know if it is a question that this Council can deal with, because if it is not I do not see why we should waste our time in discussing matters which can really have no effect. It is a question whether it is a proper question for the Council to con- sider, and upon which they can act if it is carried. Councillor Flood: I am rather surprised at the unusual course Alderman Sutton has adopted. It is not my experience that a member can get up before a motion is submitted, to ask a question. lam afraid we have not gota quorum now, but what I have got to say in reply to Alderman Sutton is this—that this resolution is a minute already embodied in the minute book of the County

Council of London, cafried under the chairmanship of Lord Rosebery. If that august body considered it advantageous to carry such a resolution as that for the protection of their own interests as' a governing body, I am not out of place in asking the Council to carry such a resolution. The TOWN CLERK: There is not a quorum.

div.p: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
THE PARISH CHURCH.

Thanksgiving services were held on Sunday. at Warrington Parish Church. There were three cele- brations of the Holy Communion—at seven a.m., eight a.m., and after morning prayer; a children's service in the afternoon, and sermons morning and evening. All the services were largely attended, especially that in the evening, when the church was crowded. The church was, as usual, very hand- somely decorated. By a illness of a member of the family, Mrs. Willis was prevented from taking part in the decorations, which was executed by Mrs. R. T. Pftirclough, Mrs. W. Woods, the Misses White, Robinson, Percival, Burgess, Allen, Chrimes, Cash, Brooks, and Boyle, assisted by the pupils from the Clergy Daughters' school and other members of the congregation. At the evening service, the choir sang Sir Frederick Ouseley's anthem—" It came even to pass." The preacher for the day was the Rev. Lloyd Jones. vicar of All Saints', Wellingborough. In the morning he based his discourse upon Deut. viii. 3. His subject at night was taken from Jer. viii. 20—" The harvest is passed, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." In closing, the preacher made an appeal on behalf of the clergy fund, to which the offertories were devoted. A sum of £6OO, he said, was required in that parish for the clergy. Of that sum £5OO were provided, and the congregation were only asked to supply the difference. It seemed to him to be an enormous propor- tion that the Rector was giving. He felt certain that, after a time, the congregation would take care that the Rector was not allowed to lose anything so out of pro- portion in that matter. He had always heard that Lan- cashire people were very true and generous, and he was quite certain that when they saw that theirclergy did not want to make money out of them, but that they wanted their souls and were willing to "spend and be spent," they would rally round them. The offertories for the day amounted to £49. The festival was continued on Tuesday evening, when the preacher was the Rev. Canon MacClure, Dean-desig- nate of Manchester. There was a large congregation. His discourse was founded upon Psalm cxlv .ILS. Before entering upon his subject he referred to the object of the offertory—the Clergy Fund. The parishioners, he said, had been told that a sum of £lOO was required to meet a sum ever so much larger for the purpose of maintaining the ministry in that place. Not a farthing of the money would ever roach, or was intended to reach, the Rector's pocket but it could not be a good thing or proper and right that, he would not say the whole burden, but that the large priveleg,e of helping to maintain the ministry in any parish should devolve either upon the patron, the clergy, or some certain individuals. The Church of Eng- land, if it was anything at all, was democratic in prin- ciple. Here was a church, which, for anything he knew to the contrary, was free and open to all. All were wel- come. It was never intended for a moment that that should be an opportunity to be basely used by persons for the purpose of relieving themselves of what he would not call responsibility, but what he believed to be one of the greatest priveleges set forth in Holy Scripture—to offer to God of our substance, the first fruits of our increase. There was a large congregation. The collections at the whole of the services amounted , to about£sB. BE WSEY-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL. This chapel was very finely decorated on Sunday, the oceasion being the harvest thanksgiving services. The decorations had been designed by Mr. George S. Pendle- bury, and were carried out under his direction by Mrs. Freeman, Mrs. Shaw Green, Mrs. Parkinson, Mrs. S. Whitehouse, Mrs. Isaac Hayward, the Misses Freeman, Beaman, Bonnell, Bennett, Jones, Shaw Green. and G. Shaw Green, and Messrs. Peudlebury, Dudley and Evans. A platform, which had been epecially erected for the convenience of the choir, which had been augmented for the occasion by an orchestra, was the chief centre of attraction. The front was graced with festoons of oats intermingled with berries, whilst suspended midway I were fine bunches of grapes. Arranged on a shelf irn= mediately below was a collection of choice plants, whilst in the centre was a varied assortment of vegetables and several large loaves of bread. Running along the bot- tom was a fringe of flowers. Over each of the entrance doors near thc pulpit was a wreath of choice dahlias. The windows, tzc., were also suitably embellished. Preaching in the morning from Galatians, vi. 9, the Rev. Thomas Ross said there were idlers and workers in the Church as well as in the world, the one being as great a curse as the others were a blessing. Work was not a degradation, it was something sacred. No one ought to be without employment of one kind or another, and the best preventive against weariness in ordinary and spiri- tual work was to live not cnly for themselves but for the benefit of others. There was a very large congregation. Special anthems and hymns were sung at each service, and collections were taken in aid of the circuit funds. In continuation of the harvest thanksgiving a fruit soiree and social gathering was held on Thursday even- ing, in the large room adjoining the Chapel. There was a large attendance. The Rev. A. Freeman presided, and in opening the proceedings expressed his pleasure at meeting so many members of the society and congrega- tion to which he has recently been appointed. Addresses were delivered by Alessi s. E. Place, J. W. Hayward, and Stanley, as representing the officials, leaders, and con- gregation. The chapel choir, under the direction of Mr. J. M. Muir, rendered a choice selection of music, and solos were given by Miss Bonnell. At the close a collec- tion was taken, and the surplus fruit sold for the benefit of the:poorer members of the congregation. CHRIST CHURCH LATCHFORD,

_ The harvest thanksg,,iving services were continued on Sunday, at Christ Church, Latchford, and were well attended. Mr. Fry was at the organ, and fulfilled his duties with his accustomed ability. A new anthem by Mr. WilliaM Johnson, of Warrington, "He bath made the earth.' was well rendered.

div.head: AMATEUR ART IN NEW JERSEY.
div.p: AMATEUR ART IN NEW JERSEY.

" Spring is here, said Leonidas Robinson, Jr., en- thusiastic amateur photographer that he is. " Nature smiles," said he. " The grass is green in the fields." The trees are leafy by rural waysides, and on swelling knolls. The hills are thick with verdure. Brooks, doubtless, are now singing blithely through sunny meads. They are also unquestion- ably roaring and rumbling among obtruding rocks, beauteous in moist mosses and spray-peat led lichens. In shadowy depths, moreover, they must now, naturally, be moaning and murmuring with plain- tive tongue; and if they are not at the same time ; widening hither and you into eddying pools, on whose tossing bosoms wanton foam flecks rise and fall in sensuous revel, then the gentle poet of the spring-time is a wan and sad-eyed liar. Such and all this being the case," said enthuasistic Leonidas, it behooves me to go forth at once and secure the shadow ere the substance perish." Whereapon he went out with his tripod and his camera, and bore down upon the sylvan suburbs of Jersey, casting an artistic eye about for choice bits, rare effects, masses of colour, and other striking things which might have strayed away from the vocabulary of the callow art critic, to his about loose on lieu soil. As he strolled, he mused. Imbued with that modest, shrinking and soulful timidity which marks the artist, he instinctively avoided those pas- toral scenes from the neighbourhood of which pre- monitory symptoms of the honest watch dog were wafted to him on the bosom of the balmy breeze, and each soft impression of the landscape that was heightened by such action as the soil-disturbing and mellifluous-voiced bull could bestow upon the pic- ture he studied from afar."

"How nature does smile to-day !" said Leonidas. " Oh, these beauties all! It exhilarates my inmost soul to drink them in ! By the way, a reminder." Leonidas drew the reminder from the inside pocket of his coat. It held a pint, and its top screwed off. It was surely a pleasant reminder : for, when Leonidas screwed the top on again, his face was wreathed in smiles. Ali ! he had the true artistic sense, had Leonidas.

And he mused as he walked, and rejoiced that he was able to keep at a safe distance all that en- dangered the serenity and peace of his contempla- tive soul, as well as his physical comfort, when sud- denly, at a turn in the quiet lane into which he had strolled, he came upon a group of citizens lying in in advanced stage of masterly inactivity, along the 1 wayside fence. "Ah," thought Leonidas, "honest and hardwork- ing sons of the plough, doubtless, snatching a moment's sweet forgetfulness from their long day of weary toil. Twill steal me quietly by, and leave them in undisturbed possession of their much- needed rest." But the hard-working sons of the plough did not appreciate Leoniiias's gentle consideration of their comfort. As the meandering artist was tip-toeing by the group, one of the party, with a fierce and stubby countenance, and grasping in his honest fist a stout and knotty club, arose from his siesta on the ' greensward, and advancing toward Leonidas said, in a husky voice: " Ali, there, Gussie ! [low does she head ?" ! Such unexpected familiarity pained Leonidas, yet lie smiled benignly, and kept on his way. But the gentleman with the club sought further con- verse with him, and the others of the group came forward and obstructed the artist's path. Then a big and growing fear took possession of his soul that the gentleman surrounding him were not the honest and hard-working ploughmen he had taken them to be, although it was plain that they were in the habitual contact with the soil.

As they stood about him, grim, ragged, dirty and leering, Leonidas not knowing exactly what would be etiquette under the circumstances, reached in his inside coat-pocket, and produced, with a trem- bling; hand, the pleasant pint reminder with a screw top, and passed it over without a word, to the - husky citizen with the club. This movement was so unexpected that it took the fellow's breath away. When he recovered himself, he turned to his com- panions, with a wink that brought his mouth and his eye in close communion, and said: A angle, pards, with manna in the wilderness! Gussie, here's yer mother-'n-law baldheaded, an' yer wife never a widder ! "

From one to the other the reminder passed until its usefulness was gone, and Leonidas was toasted affectionately as Dear Clarence, Nibsy, My Gentle Swan and Cull. Then he thanked the lively and social group, and essayed to pass on with a sickly smile and a trembling "Good-day." But the pleas- ant company of free and easy pilgrims would not hear of parting from Leonidas yet. One grim-look- ing citizen, who had music in his soul, took hold of
the shrinking artist's shoulder, and. yelled in big ear:
" Shpiel 'em up, cully ! Shpiel ! " " Yes, dear Clarence !" exclaimed another; "tune up yer three-legged ' cordeon, an' kind o' soothe us with a melojus,note or two." .

Then, whe-n Leonidas explained that his beloved Anthony outfit was not a producer of melody, but simply instruments for the pleasure and instruc- tion of the amateur artist in photography, the cit- izens drew closer to him, and said in chorus: " Oh-h-h ! ain't—that—nice !" "I am here for a day's outing," said Leonidas; "and am gathering gems of nature with the ' camera."

"Now, ain't it lucky nor nothin' that we hap- pened.along, then, Gussie ?" said the man with the club. "We're jest the gems o' nature that yer lookin' for. P'int yer gun oh us an' gather us in.' Then for an hour Leonidas was kept busy posing and photographing the jocose party. They insisted on being taken singly, in couples and in groups. They obliged the gentle, trembling and perspiring Leonidas to pose them in the tableaux of the Dying Gladiator ; Ajax Drying the Lightning ; Eve Tempt- lag Adam, in which the man with the club person- . ated Eve ; the Barefoot. Boy, and a score of siatilax subjects, until the artist's stock of plates was ex- hausted. , Then the lively, group demanded their pictures, ordering dozens of them in all styles, and insisting that the orders be filled at once, because they had no time to wait. The explanations of the unfor-- tunate amateur, that he could not perfect the pic- tures there, had no effect on the impatient patrons of art, and they were about to dump the protesting Leonidas and his outfit into the ditch, when two men in a wagon came driving along. Leonidas had gathered his kit together, and without a word he tossed it into the wagon as it came by, and threw himself in after it. "Nature may have worn a pleasant smile to-day," said he, after he had explained his situation to the( men.in the wagon; " her smile may have been ex- tremely pleasant; but she'll have to be audibly langhing when I come to Jersey °again to woo her as an amateur photographer, and I want you to be- lieve it."—From" Tramp, Tramp, Tramp!'

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL

NEW MORTGAGE DEBENTURES. The directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, as will be seen from an advertisement on our front page, are prepared to receive subscriptions for the issue of £600,000 mortgage debentures at par, payable to the Company's bankers as follows :—on application 5 per cent; allotment 20 per cent; Ist December 25 per cent ; let January 25 per cent; and Ist February 25 per cent. The subscribers, may, of course, pay up in full on allot- ment or on any date fixed for payment of an instalment. Intercst at the rate, of four per cent will accrue on the . amounts as paid up, and will be payable half-yearly. Applications for these debentures must be made on forms which are provided for the purpose, and be accompanied with a deposit of 5 per Cent on the amount applied for. Scrip will be. issued against letters of allotment after pay- ment of the amount due thereon. It should be added that the Ship Canal with its docks and railways and their revenue, as well as the Bridgewater Canals and their revenue will be the security for the borrowing. powers authorised by the Company's Acts. The invest- ment is therefore one • that can be confidently recom- mended as safe and substantial. There is every pros- pect of the Canal proving successful and it will interest investors and the general public to know that the direc- tors hope to be able to open the lower section of the Canal—that is from Eastham to Weston Point—early in 1891, and the higher sections by the time fixed for the contracts.
At Bow-st. Police Court on Thursday, !Walter Hassell was remanded, charged on his own confession with murdering Private Downey, of the King's Royal Rifles, in India.
A London contemporary understand that Mr. Parnell has been forbidden to take part in any outdoor agitation, and is compelled to exist on a strict regimen prescribed by his medical adviser.

div.head: TIT-BITS. IARRIED LIFE IN JAPAN
div.p: TIT-BITS. IARRIED LIFE IN JAPAN

The wife is but little better than the servant of the husband, and the ties of marriage and divorce are here so loose that he can dispense with beret pleasure. Marriage in Japan is not attended with the solemnity and religious ceremony of the English wedding. It is a civil contract, and the negotia- tions for it go on, as a rule, through the parents. The young man and woman have no preliminary courtship, and the seeing one another for one or two times is the only chance they have of deciding whether there is any compatibility of tempera- ment. When Yum Yum has arrived at the age of fifteen or sixteen, her parents instruct one of their friends or a professional match-maker to look about for a good husband for her. If they have decided upon the young man, they mention his name, and it is the duty of the friend to speak to the parents of the prospective bridegroom and arrange the matter. The go-between is called a Neka- dachip. He appears in every Japanese mar- riage, and it would be entirely improper for either the bridegroom or the parents to arrange a match without him. He has charge of everything relating to the marriage. He brings the young people together, generally at a tea-house, where both families meet to have a party for the occasion, and it is at this meeting that the two often see each other for the first time, If, as in the case of "The Mikado," Yum Yum falls in love at first sight with her Nanki-Poo, it is all right. The two giggle and laugh, and examine each other, and few days later, the match being agreed upon, presents pass between the two parties, and the acceptance of these presents is understood as an agreement that the marriage is to take place. The presents consist of five tubs of sake or rice wine, of five articles of food, two rolls of silk, and a silken girdle. This is, of course, among the better classes. The lower and poorer send a less amount, and a poorer quality. The ceremony proper is made up of the drinking of sake and the eating of a dinner together in the presence of the two families. The bride comes to the groom's house to be married, and she brings along presents for him and her prospective parents- in-law. She appears upon the scene in a dress of white, which, however, she changes before the ceremony for one of colours, which is a present to her from the groom. The groom also gets a present of a gown from her, and puts this on. At the drinking of the wine the bride gets the first cup, and there is an aim 03t incessant drinking throughout. the ceremony. After marriage the bride or the wife is swallowed- up, as it were, in the family of hei husband. 80010 l on the duties of woman urge her to be subservient to her parents-in-law, and in times past she was expected to communicate with her own parents chiefly by messenger, and not to visit them by any means frequently. The chief book on woman training in Japanese literature is the " 0003 Daigaku," which is taught to all Japanese girls, and on which lam told they base their conduct. It is founded on the principle that woman is much the inferior of man, and that she is naturally prone to evil. It says that nine women out of ten are suffering from mental disorders of intellect, anger and resentment, evil speakiag, jealousy, and lack of intellect. The wife should, therefore, depend upon her husband's instructions in all things, and she is subservient to her father in a like degree before marriage. She has, says this book, no right to' show jealousy, and if her husband is guilty of jai' proprieties she should gently reprove him. She should go to no place without her husband's per- mission, and a husband has the right to bring s' concubine into the house if he will. The result 01 this is that concubinage prevails here to a large a," tent, and the men of Japan have a low moral stare- ard in regard to women. The husband has almost, absolute control over his wife by the law of divorce, and he can get rid of her if he will on seven different grounds. If his wife has reached the age of 50 and is childless, he can divorce her. If she talks too much the law allows him to send her awaY if she is guilty of theft, if she is addicted to jealous' or if she is disobedient to her parents-in-law, she is liable to divorce, and if she commits adultery she is of course divorced. With such customs it is no wonder that the number of divorces in Japan i 5 larger than than those of Indiana in its palmiest dart of liberal divorce suits.

div.head: DELUDER AND THE DELUDED
div.p: THE DELUDER AND THE DELUDED

• It used to be thought that certain persons lute. peculiar faculties for curing diseases, while in many' instances charms were used for the same purpose. Dr. Armstrong relates a curious anecdote in con- nection with the latter superstition. It seems Chief Justice Holt, an English Jurist, when a young man, went to a tavern in a country town with sores friends to have a frolic, and that they did not recol- lect the fact of their having no money until thel had run up a long score. In this dilemma Holt ivee called upon to get them out of the scrape; and ob" serving that the landlord's daughter was suffering from an ague-fit, be at once collected several plants, mixed them up with a great deal of mock ceremony, rolled them up into a ball, and tied them round the girl's neck; scrawling first, hoW• ever, grotesque letters upon the piece of parchment in which the plants were wrapped. Much to the surprise of the coLjurer and his friends, the eel° departed, and the girl seemed quite well. The landlord was so grateful for the cure that he gladly made Holt a present of the bill himself and friends had run up, and even offered to pay somethlngi 5 handsome. Now the strangest part of the storY yet to be told. Some years after, when Holt promoted to the bench, a woman was brought' before him for witchcraft (the last ever tried for that offence in Englan.l), and strange as it malt I seem, she made no defence, but simply stated tba she had effected certain cures by means of a bell' which she produced. This very ball proved te be the identical one which the judge had made I"' youthful days.
