THE MURDERER OF COLONEL STEWART. A Cairo correspondent telegraphs that Suleiman, the 'murderer of Colonel J. D. Stewart, has been discovered and killed. The treacherous murder of Colonel Stewart And seizure of his wrecked steamer by Suleiman at Wady •Gama was one of the early episodes of those exciting times when Lord Wolseley's expedition was on its way towards Khartoum. The news that has now reached Cairo is that Saleh Bey, with his men, had come across • Stewart's murderer, and in the conflict which ensued • Suleiman was killed.
• IRE WORST BOYS IN WARRINGTON.

A melancholy case came before Messrs. R. Gar- nett and E. M..Crosfield, sitting at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Tuesday. Two intelli- Rent-looking lads, named William Campbell and 'John James Campbell, the former 13 and the latter 12: years of age, were brought up in custody charged With having robbed their father of the sum of Bs. 10d. 12n the previous day. The father, AlexanderlCampbell, bees in Refuge-square, and is a brewery labourer. On Sunday he was working night turn, and returned th his hoMe at about seven o'clock on Monday morning. While Sitting in a chair having a smoke, be fell asleep. At that time he had 9s. 7d. in one of the pockets of his trousers, and on awakening he discovered that Bs. 10d. of the money had been abstracted. The two lads had disappeared from the house, and he went in search of them. His quest was, however, fruitless, and he re- ported the matter at the Police Station the same morn- „lug. In the afternoon Constable Monoghan heard that Lhe lads had been seen in the neighbourhood of Stockton neath, a village about two miles distant, smoking tkgarettes, and in the evening he heard that they had been to the theatre. Towards midnight on Monday they were found sleeping in an outbuilding in Pierpoint- It. On search being made, a new purse containing ss. Was found in the possession of the older boy. They were Subiequently charged with having robbed their father, and William Campbell replied, "There was only Bs. 3d." The younger prisoner, in answer to the charge, said, " Went with him (William) and we spent it out by Wilders- 'Pool."—mv. ocorge Riley, school attendance officer, Warrington, said that the prisoners never went to ithool, and the father had frequently complained to him about their having robbed him. They were the worst ss in Warrington, and it would be a good thing if they could be sent to a reformatory school. The elder Prisoner had been ordered to the Clio, but the, doctor Would not pass him.—The father of the lads informed %a Court that this made the sixth time that they had robbed nim.—The Chairman (Mr. R. Garnett) said that he had not heard a more melancholy case in that Court. for some time, and they had to hear some very sad ones. The Bench felt it repulsive to send such young lads to Prison, but that was the ,only means by which they could pass into a reformatory. They would be im- prisoned for a fortnight, and would afterwards go to a reformatory for a period of five years.

IRE ALLEGED ATTEMPTED MURDER. AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. S. Rigby a county magistrate, Thomas Nil, a puddler, employed at. Warrington, was 'nought up on remand on a charged of having etttempted to murder a woman named Mar 3, Lyons. Rider circumstances previously reported in the EXaminer." It appears that on Monday week Lyons, 'Who belongs to Dunham Massey, and is about 40 rears of age, was in the company of the prisoner, and the two wandered to the river side near Howley, Where, it is alleged, the prisoner threw the woman into the river, after a quarrel had taken place between them. , Hall was soon afterwards taken Into custody, when he explained the circumstances ' yr saying that he and Lyons fell asleep on the ' Pass. On awakening he had occasion to accuse 4er of having robbed him, an altercation followed, ittid he pitched her into the river. Whether this be the correct version or not, there is no doubt that the woman ~Ix'as struggling in the water when her screams drew Inc attention of a number of people. A crowd collected, and by means of a long rake she was drawn from the Water. The couple were taken to the police station, and Ball was detained on a charge of attempted murder, the woman being sent to the workhouse, with the intention that next morning she should be called as a Witness against the prisoner. When Hall was brought UP on Tuesday morning, however, the woman had dis- appeared, having obtained her discharge from the work- . house early on the morning. Thereupon the county Police, assisted by the members of the borough force, tnade a vigorous search of the town in the hope of find- ing her, but were unsuccessful. There was nothing for it in consequence, but to remand the prisoner, and this Was done for a week. When the case came forward again on Tuesday, it transpired that the woman was still ,toissing, and Sergeant Barnes, of the county police, who oas the case in hand, applied for a further remand of seven days to give him an opportunity of finding Lyons. • When the case was before the magistrate on the previous Tuesday, he said, he asked a reporter who was present not to report the proceedings, as it might prevent him finding the woman; but on the following day he saw a !Von in a Warrington paper, and he could not tell how 4ar that might have assisted the woman in evading the Police.—Mr. Buckton (magistrates' clerk) : What did the teporter say ?—Sergeant Barnes : I requested him not to re,.. Port the proceedings as it might prevent me finding tier. He said, " I must put something in." "Well," I I aaid, "You will have every information after we have tried to find the woman, but I ask you not to put it in I tnatil then."—The Magistrate : What,l have to say is this. If you (the reporters) give such reports, we shall nave to keep you outside. You must not put in anything to hinder us here. The sergeant has a right to complain cLi you preventing him discharging his duties. You 'mew you have no right to be here.—The Magistrates' Clerk ; In cases of this kind.—The Magistrate : And therefore, unless you are more discreet, we shall know how to act with you in future.—The prisoner was then temanded. _

NATIONAL 'UNION OF PAPER MILL WORKERS. MEETING AT NEWTON. On Wednesday evening a meeting was held at the Legh Arms Hotel, Newton, under the auspices the Newton-le-Willows branch of the above Union. There was a fair attendance, Mr. Herring ; Presiding supported by Mr. W. Y. Jackson, secre- , tlitry of the Uuion, and Mr. D. Williams, repro- gentative of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers. The Chairman briefly introduced Mr. Jackson to those - Present, remarking that as Mr. Jackson was passing that he thought it would be a very good opportunity of making acquaintance with the district branch. Mr. Jackson, who was well received, said he was glad of the opportunity afforded him on that occasion by the Newton-le-Willows branch, of saving a few words of en- couragement to the Trades Unionists among them; and of vindicating their action in organising, as they were doing, the various paper mill workers of the country. It was ;L peat matter for congratulation, and one fraught with 'plight hopes for the future, that the operatives were responding so generally, and with so much enthusiasm to the call of the National Union. All over the country shorn the north of Scotland to the south England, °ranches were being formed, and wherever they had been established, men were found willing and able to undertake the duties of the Trades Union. (Rear, hear.) They had sprung up as though by raagie, and were becoming an exceeding great army, The Union was now a great fact, universally and financially, and had a great future before it. The men who had taken it up, were not going to look backwards, or take • their hands from the stilts of the plough, but they would gG on breaking up the fallow ground of past neglect, and 4°, wing seeds of brotherhood, where the rank weeds of Individualism and selfishness had too long destroyed occupation. They would toil on, on behalf of the rights 41ad the dignity of labour, and in the defence of British Industry, till they reaped their harvest, in rescuing the trade from the rifts of unprincipled competition, and amelioriated the condition both of labour and capital. (Applause.)—Alluding to the difficulties they had to con- tend with, Mr. Jackson said that they not unfrequently encountered opposition. Some firms had taken alarm at the prospect of having to reckon with associated labour, Arid had gone the length, in the spread of intimidation, and a state of panic, of preventing organisation, and even of suppressing branches. That such a thing was Possible was only another proof of the necessity of vindi- tating, even so late in the day, the independence of the „Workinen, and they would not tolerate a state of matters In which working people were being treated as serfs or triminals, and compelled to accept employment on con- ditions which deprived them of their birthright as British titizens,and placed their lives and their happiness, and that s°f their families at the mercy of tyrannical task masters. Ao doubt much of the alarm under such circumstances ...vras due to an unfounded trade, and the action of the Union, and he wished very plainly to Say, that everyone 1:4 them, as workmen would fully consider the difficult Position in which their employers had been placed, these Past years, on account of our mischievous and ruinous trade policy. But they were entitled to demand that the Workman was not to be made the bleeding sacrifice to •atone for the mistakes of trades and politicians. (Hear rkear.) Dividends and profits had suffered, and they Were assailed in the fierce competition that had been rlaile- on, but they were determined that the lives of the glish operatives, were worth concerning and would be F•cncerned, and some other way of discovering and adopt- tag, of making fairlprofit the capital. He had to corn- Plainer the disorganisation and the individualism, which "ad characterised their industry, both on the part of ckalployers, and managers, and of the workman, they 'a4l sacrificed and surrendered the independence of their position as producers, to the middleman. It was to this 7.,:steful, expensive and unprincipled machinery of dis- lbution, that they had to contribute the intolerable ;oinditions they were now endeavouring to remedy, If C labour and the capital associated in fair partnership la their improved industry, had properly looked after the RGod of the whole, instead of blindly and treacherously

pursuing an individual policy of selfish aim, they would have served the people better, and secured better returns to both employers, and employed. Mr. Jackson then explained at some length the mercantile aspect of trade in this connection, and quoted instances in illustration of the manner in which the paper mills were kept down in detail, in competition for orders from middlemen, and the conditions of subjec- tion to their demands, and opportunities which in Wany cases existed in modern business. -He said that they as workmen were interested in altering this, and having the inderendence of the producers vindicated. They knew that wages were not paid out of capital, but out of profits, and they also knew to their cost, that labour must suffer in the end, and had suffered on account of nefarious trading. They were combining to resist this in the future, to the uttermost. Their Union., therefore, *as a protection to capital associated in fair partnership with labour, as well as to labour itself. (Cheers.) No sensible, fair-minded employer had anything from their Union, and none ot thew, he was bound to say, did fear it, and he was certain they would find that their best safeguard for the peaceable and profitable pursuit of their business, would be in the coercive and educative power, which a united body of intelligent workpeople could afford them in putting an end to the immoral and degrading practices which flourished unchecked, and in- satiated in the name of business, watered by the ruin of firms, and the blood and the sorrows of labourin,g men l and women. (Cheers.) He warned them that the economy of trade was wrong, it was inhuman, and abominably selfish.. He counselled them to protect the interests of labour, and to stand by their order. They did not despise or repine at their lot of toil, but they asserted their right to defend its honour, and to bequeath to their children, to their country, and their class, an improved heritage, a heritage in which their lives in all respects would be worth living. (Loud cheers.) Mr. D. Williams, of Earlestown, was exceedingly pleased to have come in contact with Mr. Jackson, and the address they had heard ought to be all sufficient to stimulate them in their own organisation. He concluded by moving a vote of thanks to '.Mr. Jackson, which was heartily accorded, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: DISASTROUS EXPLOSION IN AMERICA.
div.p: DISASTROUS EXPLOSION IN AMERICA.
ELEVEN PERSONS KILLED.

Nsw YORK, TTIESDAY.-At four o'clock this afternoon several terrific explosions occurred in quick succession at the Dupont Powder Works near Wilmington, Delaware. The whole section known as the upper yard was com- pletelywrecked, and it is feared that at least ,ten of the workmen have been killed and twenty injured. One of the magazines exploded first, and the rolling and drying mills near by were set off by the concussion. Nearly every dwelling in the neighbourhood is reported to be damaged, and the explosions startled the inhabitants for many miles around. Further particulars of the explosion at the powder mills near Wilmington state that the dead were all employes. Several workmen are still missing, and are believed to have been blown to atoms. Some of the members of the firm were injured, among them being Mr. Eugene Dupont, the chief proprietor, but none sus- tained serious hurt. The Dupont mills extend along the Brandywine river for a distance of .two miles, within which space there are fifty houses inhabited by the workpeople. All of these dwellings were wrecked, and the force of the explosion was so great that the windows of the houses in several parts of Wilmington Were shattered. . .

NEW Yonx, WEDNESDAY EvEntno.—The latest advices from Wilmington place the number of persons killed at eleven, including art aged woman who was crushed be- neath the falling roof of a house wrecked by the ex- plosion. The other victims were workmen employed in the mills, who, with the exception of three, were blown to pieces, only fragments of their bodies being, found. The theory which finds most credit as to the cause of the catastrophe is, that the explosion originated in the soldering-iron which one of the victims was using to solder the tin covers of the powder canisters being too hot, and firing the powder. The operation has always been known as an extremely dangerous one,and the man referred to was the only hand trusted to perform it.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOAIiD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOAIiD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting ot this body was held on Wednesday, at the Board-room at the Workhouse. The chair PM occupied by Alderman Harrison, and there were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, And Messrs. G. Ratcliffe, R. Heaton, E. Aukland; A. Jolley, J. Clarke, J. Dignum, S. Davies, J. Dobson, W. Houghton, J. Humphreys, T. Jones, T. Mather, J. Turton, P. Warburton, H. Hibbert, W. Gill, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (workhousa master), and H. M. Mines (superintendent of the Padgate schools.)

sows costiarrraa. This Committee recommended that a new cooking apparatus be obtained iii place of the present open fire- place, the Master to obtain prices of the most improved apparatus. It was also recommended that the following tenders be accepted :—Roberts and Son ,boots and shoes; Evans, drapery; Percival, groceries; and the " Observer" Company, printing and stationary.—The minutes were adopted without discussion.

div.head: PAD TB SCHOOLS COMMITTEE._
div.p: PAD TB SCHOOLS COMMITTEE._
The Committee recommended the Board to adopt the tender of Abel Pickavance for a supply of leather. The doctor reported the health of the children to be good.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES COMILITTIIIS.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES COMILITTIIIS.

The report of this Committee stated that fess had been allowed in 13 cases, all of which were old. 14,1 r. Jones, in proposing the adoption of the minutes, remarked that there *as a decrease in the number of applications for school fees. He did not know whether that was an in- dication of good trade, or an indication that the Com- mittee dealt with a firm hand in order to prevent being imposed upon.—The minutes were then confirmed. •
A RESIGNATIOW.
Mr. James Ball, assistant-schoOlmaster at Padgate, sent in his resignation of that position, which was accepted.

LT/NACY STATISTICS. A short discussion took place with regard to the pauper lunatics with whom tho Board had to deal, and the CLERK said that the question might eventually arise for providing at the Workhouse separate accommoda- tion for certain cases. In reply to a question Mr. SHEARER said that there were from that Union, in:Rain- hill, Prestwich, and other asylums, 137 patients.

THE QUESTION OF NEW OFFICES. Mr. AIIKIAND brought forward a proposition to the effect that Union offices, Board-room, and Committee rooms be provided in a central part of Warrington. He considered that the present offices were not fit for the work. They were unhealthy, and were not fit to be used by the general public. The rent the Board now paid for the public offices was £145 per annum, and he estimated that a new building would cost about £2,500, including site.—The CHAIRMAN: You think if the an- nual rents were capitalised, it would pay us ?—Mr. AU/I- LAND : If we could induce the overseers to erect a por- tion of the offices, we should be in pocket. I think all the offices should be in one building.—The CHAIRMAN : I do not think that we should be embarrassing ourselves in the least by adopting the principle that new offices should be built.—Mr. HEATON said that he thought the time had arrived when the Board should have good offices, and he had great pleasure in seconding the pro- position.—Mr. DonsoN : My impression is that the cost would be about £4,500. Probably the Guardians will not be in existence two years from now.—The CHAIR- MAN: I hope we shall all be living. (Laughter.)—Mr. DOBSON : We may be living, but not as a Board of Guardians. Mr. Sutton's argument is, that possibly the business of the Council, and of the Board of Guardians might be concentrated together, and the Guardians dis- pensed with.—Mr.Jou.xy : How does Mr. Sutton know? —The CLERIC said that there could be no two opinions as regarded the advisability of providing new buildings. but local government was at present in a chaotic con- dition. When the County Councillors Bill was intro- duced in Parliament it contained provisions for forma- tion of district Councils. So great were the difficulties in Parliament that the Government found it necessary to cut the Act into two, andto be content for the session to provide County Councils, leaving over the question of local or district Government, and of district Councils, for another session. There was a very divided opinion as to the combination of the existing Local Government, and as to the provision of distinct local areas for government purposes, and under the circumstances he felt it his duty to point out the possibilities of the future.—Mr. 11.vrcLivrE said that he was not against the proposals, but under the circumstances he could not see his way to support it.— Mr. W. HEATON said that the sooner they could get new offices the better. Their Clerk looked well, but he was the only one in the offices who did. (Laughter.) The Board should perform its duty irrespective of what might happen in the future. If he was their clerk he should have better offices.—The CLERK said he was perfectly , sensible of the additional comfort that would be secured. He rather held the view that Boards of Guardians would , not be interferred with, but still it was his duty to re- mind them that it was at present an uncertainity-.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON proposed, and Mr. HIBBERT seconded, that , no steps be taken in the matter at present, and this amendment was carried by 12 votes to six. -

THE POOR-LAW CONFERENCE. The CLERIC read a paper on the recent Poor Law Con- ference, which he attended, and at the close was accorded a vote of thanks for his services. During a conversation that followed, he remarked that he believed that it was a fact that if all the paupers in England were marched five abreast, in regular marching order, they would form a procession a hundred miles in length. Mr. Sutton also referred to a paper written by Dr. Benger, 'on the subject of how to deal with and lessen this pauperism.

At Witnessham, near Ipswich, on Thursday morning, a widow named Dixon, and her son, were found in their house with their throats cut, the widow being dead and the son nearly so. A letter was previously found on a neighbour's doorstep from the son,announcing his inten- tion to commit the double crime. The son recovered consciousness, and said he had attempted poisoning before cutting his throat. Be may recover.

A SPELLING BEE NEEDED AT WARRINGTON. Sir,—l should like to know if it is true that a promi- nent member a the Town Council, and a luminary light °O. of the Watch Committee,lately went to different inhabit. tants of the town, pointing out what he believed to be —7. serious errors ,in spelling in a document recently issued by our Town Clerk ; one of the errors being that the Town Clerk had spelled the word "intitoled," whereas it ought to have been "entitled" (go said the luminary), and another error being that he had spelled the word " alleging" wrongly, as it ought, he said, to have been spelled " alledging.' Surely, if this be true, the indivi- dual shonldtake some private lessons in spelling, or per- haps he might try and teach the Town Clerk the new style which is peculiarly his own.—Yours truly, A. B. C.
THE FLABBINESS OF TIIE WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

Sir,—At the meeting of the Town Council,on Tuesday, when in the order of business Councillor Flood should have proposed a motion, he was prevented doing so by an unseemly interruption on the part of the ex-Mayor, thus providing the Tory party with an opportunity of bolting, which they took advantage of in a manner highly suggestive of a pre-determination to insult Coun- cillor Flood, and through him the working-men of War-

-rington. This incident ought to be an object lesson to working-men, as it shows an utter absence of sympathy on the part of the Tories with those who are compelled to earn their daily bread, and furnishes convincing proof of the necessity of all sections of the labour party com- bining for the purpose of securing to themselves a more equitable share of those representative offices which have the power of affecting movements having for their ob- ject the improvement of the condition a those whose right to exist depends upon their daily toil. I suggest this, and leave the issue in the hands of the working-men of Warrington, feeling ussured that they will insist upon ani reparation for the wrong done them. I think the Council acted a coward ts part in refusing to discuss Councillor Flood's motion. 'it ,was in order, definite in meaning, and had been adopted by the Lon- don County Council in its entirety. lam sure that the exhibition of flabbiness, on Tuesday, will be considered by all sensible men as a sign of mental weakness and as an evidence of the jelly-fish character of those who were elected for the purpose of carrying on the business of the town. In conclusion, let me urge the electors•to watch very closely a section of the Council which exists for the pur- pose of conserving the privileges of publicans and further- ing the interests of brewers.—YoursAc., K.

"WORKING-MEN'S HOME 'UNION." Sir,—Many of your readers who object to payin heavy rents for unsanitary houses and are unwilling to be burdened with the extra rates (as they would be with the ground rents), of those houses and shops which are now tenantless, in many cases, because the landlords will not accept a moderate rent—will not be surprised to learn that some London ,landlords are hurriedly com- bining to form a" House Owners' Protection league," They do not seem to be aware ; (1.) That the Working-men's Home Union" has been .founded and will be continued, solely upon the lines of a :thoroughly honest relation between landlord and tenant. . (2.) That its leading principles are, that no higher •percentage on the value of the houses than is charged as rent to middle class tenants shall be demanded from .working class tenants, and that the same arrangements :and cenyeniences really necessary for the health, com- fort and decency of family life shall be provided equally for one class of tenants as for the other.. (3.) That some landlords who are willing to charge moderate rents, and to keep their property in thorough repair and now joining this Union. They begin to realise the fact that just as the Union will strenuously oppose all rack renting and negligent landlords and .agents, so will it act as a powerful protection against dishonest tenants who, by defrauding suck landlords of their fair rents and wilfully destroying their property , .are among the worst enimies of the working classes, and .do very much to establish and maintain the high rentals that more honest tenants are called upon to pay. The arrangements of the Union are now in thorough corder, and good work has already been done in unsani- tary parts of London. There is no tee or payment de- manded for membership of the Union. Lam quite pre- pared to start local branches in every Working-men's .! Club in 'London, and in all the large towns and cities of England. Any number of membership forms, Sm., will be forwarded post free, on written application to me at International College Finchley-road, London.—Your 4blig,ed servant,

div.head: JAMES HAYSMAN, President of the Union.
div.p: JAMES HAYSMAN, President of the Union.
THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS.

- _ Sir,-1 enclose copy of a letter I addressed to the Town Clerk, on Tuesday last, and copy of his reply, which kindly publish. I may say in reference to the approaching Municipal Elections that it is arranged to contest the St. John's and HoWley Wards with Independent Candidates, unless one of the Political Contesting Candidates in each Ward pledges himself to do his beet to suppress the nuisance, if necessary by closing the Depots, in which case of course my friends and myself will support him.—Yours faithfully, H. J. LalloToN. 15, Upper Bank-St. Warrington, 9th October, 1890. LETTER TO THE TOWN CLERIC.] 15, Upper ank-st., Warrington, 7th October, 1890. Dear sir,-.-! have had such serious and constant corn, plaints from my tenants of the nuisance arising from the Manure Depa in Lythgoes-laue that I am compelled to write and demand that they may be permitted to breathe pure air. If the nuisance goes on, I shall take legal pro- ceedings to close the works, as I am losing money in tenants leaving and the selling value of my property is seriously diminished. When I withdrew my opposition at the Enquiry at the Town Hall, it was solely on the ground that I was assured that the contemplated expenditure would remove the nuisance. I think I have now waited long enough for the experiments to have had a fair trial, and there is no doubt that they have entirely failed. Please bring this letter forward in the proper quarter, and oblige.—Yours faithfully, H. J. LONGTON, J. Lyon Whittle Esq., Town Clerk, Warrington,
[TOWN CLERICS REPLY.] Town Clerk's Office, Warrire,ton 7th October, 1890.
Dear sir,—l am in receipt (if your letter of to-day's date which I will lay before the Sanitary Committee on Wednesday next, and let you have their decision there- on.
I may inform you that the Medical Officer of Health is instructed to report upon the condition of the depot you complain about.--Yours faithfully, J. LYON WHITTLE.
H. J. Longton Esq., Solicitor, Warrington.
THE ANNUAL ELECTION OF RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS.

Sir,—l trust that you will give me an opportunity of correcting some gross mis-statements made tsy your cor- respondent ",Ratepayer," with regard to the expenses incurred by the various Returning Officers appointed to conduct the annual elections of Commissioners. I have a feeling of repugnance in dealing with a person who has not the manliness to sign his name to ally observa- tions ise'rnay think fit to make in public affairs. How- ever, xis he has given inaccurate information, I feel it incumbent on me to correct him. He states that the expenses connected with these elections have almost trebled since 1835. I furnish below the alleged expenses side by side with the actual expenses as set forth in the Commissioner's Ledger, and which have been certified as correct by the Government auditor. Alleged Actual Expenses. Expenses. £sd R d 1885 Mr. Shaw 1886 Mr. Dobson 8 9 0 1887 .„ 1888 Mr. Fisher 1889 Mr, Lightbum 12 0 0 1890 " „ 17 90 You see, sir, that "Ratepayer" is evidently a prentice hand, and that his first attempt to act in the capacity of public mentor has been an unfortunate one. If he goes to the wrong source for his information that is his look out. As Jam writing, I may as well refer to the dinner which was given to the Board's officials in connection with the late election. The expenses of that dinner were not over 16s. per head as has been stated by your cor- respondeats. There were several officials present who had not been engaged in the election, and the cost was 75. per head. This can be verified, if my assurance is not sufficient. I know that I speak the minds of the other officers concerned when I say that we are perfect- ly indifferent as to whether we have a dinner at the ratepayers' expense or not. I think I may assure the ratepayers of Runcorn that if they, acting in good faith, wish for any information in the affairs of this Board, and will apply in the right quarters, they will be courteously received. On the other hand, as public officials are necessarily subjected to public criticism, there is no reason why that criticism should be worded in mislead- ing and offensive terms such as have characterised some of the recent effusions of your correspondentt.—l am, Sir, yours faithfully, E. MARSHALL. Town Ball, Waterloo-rd., Runcorn, 9th Oct., 1830.

div.head: FATHER MATHE W AND WARRINGTON.
div.p: FATHER MATHE W AND WARRINGTON.

Sir,—At a time when many admirers of Father Mat- hew are rejoicing to celebrate the centenary of his birth, which occurs to-morrow (Friday), there may be some who will be reminded with interest of the part taken by Warrington in promoting the Father Mathew Fund. The originator of that honourable fund is happily still alive, in the person of the Rev. Thomas mocks, 8.A., F.R.S., who now resides at Clifton, near Bristol. During his ministry at Cork, Mr. Hincks was brought into early and intimate association with the Apostle of Temperance, and, he is, therefore, entitled to speak with , direct knowledge of his character and also of his work. He left Cork in the summer of 1844, to become the,minis- ter of Cairo-st. Chapel, Warrington, where his short but useful settlement is remembered with affection, net only by old members of the congregation, but by others in, the town as well. Having occasion to lecture on Father Mathew, on Mon- day last, I was privileged to receive from Mr. Hiccks, a very helpful letter of personal recollections, and a wel- come confirmation of certain local facts. In the belief that these recollections will not be without interest to readers of your paper, and to temperance advocates in particular, and as the letter in question has already, by permission, been made public, I venture to send you the following extract.—l am, faithfully yours, FRANK K. FREESTON.

Warrington, October 9th, 1890. [co FY.] "During my settlement at Cork (my first settlement after leaving college) I became acquainted with Father Mathew, who resided there, and from whom I received many kindnesses. I had great opportunity of studying his most interesting character, and his marvellous work. Young man as I was, and Unitarian minister into the bargain, he gave me many proofs of his warm personal regard. I mention this to show that I was favourably placed for learning what he really was. I found in him the most transparent simplicity of character, great ten- derness of heart, absolute self-denial, an entire freedom from self-seeking, and a most fervent devotion to the work which he believed had been appointed for him by God. He was truly called the Apostle of the Temperance movement, and he was also its martyr. When he be- came involved in pecuniary difficulties, which threatened the destruction of his usefulness, the state of his affairs was brought to my knowledge by some mutual friends, and he subsequently furnished me himself with a full ex- planation of the facts of the case. The Inquirer: for which I was then working with my father, took the matter up, and started the fund which extricated thirn from his difficulties, and restored him to his work. It is to this, I think, that you refer in your letter. This would take place before my settlement at Warring- ton, but I find in The Inquirer' for December, 7th, 1844, a report of a public meeting in Warrington on the 29th November in that year, to promote a subscription in aid of the Mathew Fund, at which I had the pleasure of moving the first resolution, and explaining the facts. So Warrington took its share in the movement. These recollections are very hastily written, but they may possibly be of service to you in connection with your lecture.—Believe me, very sincerely yours, THOMAS HINCKS. Rev. Frank K. Freeston."

THE "GRIFFIN" HOTEL, EARLESTOWN. Sir,—All lovers of fair-play and strict honesty must re- joice that our magistrates refused to rob the proprietor of the above hotel of his license, and so administered a well-deserved snub to those fussy meddlers who seem to swarm about Earlestown, who profess " goody-goody- ness," and who parade their Chadband-like professions in public prints— " A mere professor, spite of all hia cant, is Not one whit better than a Mantis,— An insect of what clime I cant determine, That lifts its paws most parson-like, and thence, By simple savages—through sheer pretence— Is reckon'd quite a saint amongst the vermin?' If I go into a shop, and buy a watch, that watch is mine. Similarly, if Igo into a Government office and buy a license, for whatever purpose, that license is mine also. Then, if a man comes and steals my watch, he is a thief; and if he robs me of my license, by word or deed, what else is he ? There it is, as plain as a pike-staff, and the individual "who can't see it," should look up the Bth Commandment, and when found, "make a note on." But why do these " irrepressibles" confine their atten- tion only to public-houses, and leave clubs alone? The landlord of a hotel pays a large quota to the revenue, and is worried in proportion; but a club, where the same things are carried on, with no limit whatever as to closing time, can do as it pleases, and pays nothing to the State! This is the sort of khing the "faddists" wink at. But,

"I do confess, that I abhor and shrink From schemes, with a religious willy-nilly. That frown upon St. Giles's sins, but blink The peccadilloes of all Piccadilly t" Again, I thank those magistrates for their just and righteous decision ; and for "sitting on" those who would "take the mote out of another's eye, before re- moving the beam out of their own." And now a few words on a " profitless " subject viz., the letter that appeared in your columns last Satur- day, under the heading of "The Griffin License, Earles- town." I say " profitless," because it is about as jumbled a mass of incongruities as can well have been put together ; and only that the writer professes to be a "local optionist ; (or translated truly, if freely an impertinent meddler in others' concerns.) I should say he had been at several breweries before he penned it, and had indulged in several "drunks" at each one! Why, sir, he travels all over space from heaven to hell ; from a schoolboy motto .(which be doesn't understand !) to the secret eciences ; and from " local options" to " rotten eggs!" As for the two last paragraphs, they are "confusion or confounded," and are as germane to any letter of the previous week, as a eun-dial would be to a studious bull; and I only con- ceive them being written to air the author's conceit, and his superficial and misleading knowledge of scripture and heathen mythology, in both of which he proves his lamentable ignorance. Finallv "J. H. Profit" says he "holds a commission in her Majesty's service ; " and for the sake of ills honour and integrity, I hope it is not in the excise ; for, if he does, he is scouting at his own "bread and butter," and has forgotton the old saw— if, indeed, he ever knew it—that It is a very dirty bird that fouls its own nest." sth October, 1890.
PLUTO.
THE GRIFFIN LICENSING MOCKERY.

Sir,—A short time ago I heard an ex-cabinet minister speak in Liverpool. In his opening remarks he made a slight reference to the temperance question, and I was quite surprised to hear the thundering applause which greeted his passing allusion. It sounded to tne like the

div.head: liga! paLtat. I V J 44 tf•At./ g TIIE EXAMINER, SATTJRDAY, OCTOBER 11,1890
div.p: liga! paLtat. I V J 44 tf•At./ g TIIE EXAMINER, SATTJRDAY, OCTOBER 11,1890

doom of the present licensing system. The end cannot be far. The Newton magistrates have just hammered down a good strong nail into their own coffin. The law says that the drink traffic should be regulated according to the wants of the neighbourhood. But the Newton decision is in direct defiance of the voice of the people. On what grounds them was the license allowed? In reading your report, I see it 'was in deference to some shadowy commercial travellers. So evidently the Griffin is not intended for the inhabitants of Earlestown, but for outsiders. Who are these commercial travellers? I suppose they will include all and sundry gentry who, come to Eariestown to solicit votes at times of election. There is astother class, namely, those who travel the streets and 'ornament the corners on Friday evenings, but I thought they generally managed to be put up in specially reserved apartments where they get board, lodging, and liveried servants for nothing. Mr, Gillespie, whom the "Manchester Guardian" credited with a colossal imagination, candidly admitted that -" if it had been an application for a new license it would have been rdf used.' As a rule I dislike those arguments which avoid any case under consideration by hiding themselves under an "if." It is always prefer- able to deal with things as they are, and not as they would be "if" they were otherwise. However, as it now stands, the above admission is plainly against the grant- ing of the trander because it says positively that a new license would'be refused, and surely a removed license must be equally obnoxious on the very same spot and should be similarly refused. From whati can learn, the magistrates simply lacked moral courage to do what the people rightly demanded. Let them note what has been done at Bewdley. There the licensing justices absolutely declined to renew several old licenses on the ground that there were already too many ptiblic-houses. I am afraid the three Newton magistrates are helping to make the Litany a dead letter when it prays "that it may please Thee to bless and keep the magistrates, giving them grace to execute justice and to maintain truth." lam sure all the people join heartily in the response "We beseech Thee to hear us, good Lord." Then the magistrates ought also to consider that the house-they licensed is held under a system which prac- tically evades the law. Under such a system the publi- can, who ought to be the responsible person, is merely an instrument in the hands of the brewer. I was talking with a Liverpool publican the other day, and he told me that he did not even keep possession of the license- document; the brewer told him he had no right to it, and that it must be kept up at" Lord Bung's" office. What a ridiculous state of affairs; licensed premises to be without a license on the premises. The law becomes as so much waste paper. With regard to the stuff that is usually sold at such places! believe Bass's Pale and Guiness's Extra are pro- hibited and the publican is compelled to sell the brewer's mixture of" Lamb's wool " or " Mountain dew." Things are awfully mixed up. "Abortive, monstrous, and unkindly mixed; Griffins. and hydras, and chimeras dire."

If the tied-house system goes on much further, the brewers will take to erecting drink pillars where, on dropping in aid., an iron hand will hold out a full glow- ing bowl. Then then the magistrates can remain hand and glove as at present with the big brewers, and wreak their legal vengeance on the iron image itself for sup- plying drink to a man already drunk. Referring to this tied system " The Methodist Times " says—" It is a modern dodge which brings misery and ruin to all con- cerned. It is a gross injustice to that unhappy wretch who is the nominal holder of the license, because he is compelled to buy his liquor, often at a high price, from the brewer to whom the house belongs, and is ruined unless he succeeds in selling enough tosatisfy the brewer's greed. One result of the Newton case will be that the right settlement of this vexed question willbe hastened, and it will teach the people how to vote at elections. The sooner it is settled the better because the present system is nothing, but an absolute sham and a mockery.—Yours truly, Oct. 6th, 1890.
J. H. PROFIT.
in place of Mrs. J. R. Frith and Mrs. Fielding, who had left the town. Mr. F. A. Lake was re-elected treasurer. The customary vote of thanks concluded the proceed- ings.

div.head: FRODSEIAM.
div.p: FRODSEIAM.

HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICES. Sermons were I preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Frodshatn, on Sunday, by the Rev. H. Davenport, and as on similar previous occasions, the chapel had been neatly decorated with flowers, fruit, &c. The services were brought to a close on Monday evening, when a public meeting was held and several addresses delivered.

FUNERAL OF A VOLUNTEER.—On Tuesday afternoon last, the remains of Mr. John Blythe, lately residing at Volunteer-st., Frodsham, were carried to their resting place. The funeral cortege left the deceased's house shortly before three o'clock for Frodsham Parish Church, the coffin being wrapped in the Union Jack. On it were placed the deceased's helmet and wreaths of flowers, and it was borne on the shoulders of four of his comrades of the 2nd Cheshire Regiment (I Company). It was pro- ceeded by a number of members under the charge of Colour-Sergeant Davies and Sergeant-Instructor Evans, accompanied by the Frodsham Military Band, the rela- tives and friends following in the rear. On arriving at the churchyard the procession was met by the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., who read the burial service. After the coffin had been lowered into the grave the firing party in attendance fired the usual volleys. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES —The monthly meeting of the Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship Parochial Committees was held in the overseers' office, Frodsham, last evening week, when there were present—Colonel Ashton in the chair), Dr. Robinson, Messrs. T.. Lewis, W. C. Collinson. H. Tiley, and James Percival. The Clerk produced and read a copy of notice which had been forwarded to the Frodsham Gas and Water Co., requesting them to pro- vide an efficient supply of water to the township of Frodsham, also letter from the Secretary to the Company acknowledging his receipt. Instructions were given to the Inspector of Nuisances to have the pipe at the Five Crosses fountain remedied ; also that he served notice cu the owner of certain houses in Chapel-lane to provide a supply of water. The Inspector produced a set of plans from Mr. William Owen, architect, Warrington, of a house proposed to be erected at the Five Crosses, for Mr. Nath. Greening, and the same being in accordance with the byelaws in force, it was recommended that they be presented to the central authority for approval.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
SANKEY HARRIERS.

Sankey Harriers held .......g run on Satur- day. Thirteen members turned out for a run of eight miles over splendid cross country, taking in the districts of Sankey, Bold, Burtonwood, and return- ing by Bewsey after an enjoyable run. THE BEV, E. S. JACKSON.

To-day (Saturday), the Rev. E. S. Jackson, vicar of Sankey, will start on a three months tour to the West Indies, on board the "William Cliff" from Liverpool. Mr. Jackson, who is in failing health, preached a farewell sermon in the Penketh Mission Church on Wednesday evening. LIR ART CLASS.

Owing to the sn;;.-ll Wti-n;bei-o-f-4udents who at- tended at the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Saturday evening, the re-opening of the above class for the season- was postponed for a week. Last year over 20 students sat for examination, but it is hoped that the number will be considerably augumented this year. The secretary of the class is Mr. A. H. Robin- son.

div.head: BAND OF HOPE MEETING.
div.p: BAND OF HOPE MEETING.

_ On Friday evening, a meeting of the Committee and friends interested in the Band of Hope was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, for the purpose of electing officers and arranging meetings for the coming session. Mrs. It. Garnett was elected pre- sident ; vice-president, Mrs. Walker; secretary, Mr. W. T. Wilkinson; treasurer, Mr. A. J. White ; Miss Moses, Miss Mabel Garnett, and Miss E. Hob- son have charge of the music ; recitations, Miss Mainley, Miss Garnett, and Miss Walker ; Corn-. mittee, Messrs. R. Garnett, B. Hobson, W. B.Moston, Mrs. Coop, and all the officers. MUTUAL IMPROVEMET ASSOCIATION. On Wednesday the first sessional meeting of the Penketh Mutual Improvement Association.was held in the day schools, Penketh. The first paper (given by the president for the session, Mr. Thos. Gandy) was upon the past and present history of Penketh. The subject was extremely interesting, and although the paper was necessarily a short one, a great deal of matter was embodied in it.' Mr. Gandy informed his hearers that many noted men of the times had claimed connection with the place, including Mr. John Bright, Mr. Edmondson (the inventor of rail- way tickets), Mr. Warrington Wood, and others. Refreshments in the shape of coffee and biscuits were provided by Mr. and Mrs. T. Gandy and Mr. and Mrs. C. E. Parker. The meeting was thoroughly enjoyed by the hundred members present, and there was every indication of a successful season for the society. Many new names were proposed for , membership.

div.head: LYME
div.p: LYME

MUSIC AT THE CROSS.—The Lymm Church of England Brass Band played several selections of sacred music at the Cross on Sunday afternoon. WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—A meeting in connection with the above society was held in the schoolroom, on Monday evening. There were about 100 present. Mr. Collier conducted. _ _ .

MANCHESTER CITY MisstoN.—On Tuesday, Mrs. McGill invited about 100 members of the Manchester City Mis- sion to Lymm, and ontertained them at the Institute. Dinner and tea were provided, and the evening was spent in an enjoyable manner. CONGREGATIONAL THANKSGIVING SERVlCES.—Thanks- giving seivices for the safe ingathering of the harvest were held in the Congregational chapel, on Sunday, when special sermons were preached by the pastor' the Rev. Charles Clay, and suitable hymns were sung by the chDir and congregation. The church had been prettily deco- rated for the occasion, corn, flowers, and fruit had been most artistically arranged, and the effect produced was charming. The pulpit, which had been decorated by Miss Bedell, and upon which much labour had been ex- pended, looked charming in its floral garb. It was almost hidden with choice white flowers and maidennair ferns. whilst suspended from each panel was a fine bunch of black grapes. The window sills had been tastefully adorned by the Misses Dutton, Bowen, and Midgley. Collections were made during the day on behalf of foreign missions. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT THE PARISH CHURCH—The an- nual harvest thanksgiving services were held in the Parish Church, on Sunday, when the morning and even- ing preacher was the Rev. J. Ray, rector of Ashton-on- Mersey. The congregations were large, and collections were taken on behalf of the fund for the erection of the church bells. There was an early celebration of the holy communion, and in the afternoon a children's ser- vice was held, conducted by the Rector, the Rev. G. W. Guest. The Lymm .C.E.T.S. Brass Band accompanied the singing. The decoration of the transepts had been done by Mrs. Bayley, and the other windows had been adorned with a variety of corn, fruit, flowers, and foli- age by Miss Battersby, Mrs. Gibbs, Miss Jones, and Miss Norris. The Misses Howe had charge of the pulpit, and the font was very effectively decorated by Mrs. T. P. Norris. The screen was the work of the Rector and Madame Ruhle. The communion table was adorned by Mrs. Guest, and the rails by Mr. Bla.kernore.

THE RUNCORN DISTRICT NURSE FUND. The annual meeting of subscribers was held in the Town Hall, on Monday, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Wood. The Chairman presented the Committtee's report, which stated that during the Past year 185 persons have been nursed; 3,122 visits had been paid; 737 visits had been made to typhoid cases, 1,071 surgical cases ; 1,314 medical cases, and there had been 40 deaths. Nurse Evans had so dis- charged her duties as not only to win the regard of the public, but also to earn for the Worcester Institution which sent her, and for the system of outdoor nursing generally a hearty appreciation. The question of per- manent support was tne for the Committee to care- fully consider. They were in possession of a small capi- tal which it would perhaps be desirable to invest. Their ability to do this must depend upon the increase of subscribers of large and small sums.—The report was approved, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mrs. Joule. Mr. F. A. Lake, the hon, treasurer, presented the statement of accounts showing total receipts of £345 6s. Bd., which included £lO 13s. 9d. from Tableaux ; £197 12s. Ild, from the bazaar; and £43 I.Bs. Id. from football match. The chief donations were: Canon Heron, £5 ; Mr. Speikman, £5; Mr. R. Abel. £5; and the principal subscriptions were: Rev. Canon Wood, £25; Mr. T. A. Walker, £10; Mr. C. Wigg, £2 25.; and the following each contributed a guinea :—Mrs. Marwood, Dr. MacLennan, Messrs. W. Haves, S. Taylor, W. Whittaker, E. Imison, 3. J. Hewitt, J. W. Lightburn, J. J. W. Potter, F. A. Lake. Mrs. Pres- ton, Misses Mack, and Mr. W. Mellor each subscribed 10s. 6d. The expenditure amounted to £7B 2s. sd. and there was a balance in the treasurer's hands of £67 4s. 3d. The accounts of the "beef tea fund" were also presented.—Mr. S. W. Lightburn, who had audited the accounts moved that the balance should be passed, in order to show the undenominational character of the work of the nurse he gave the following statistics. The nurse had visited 185 sick persons. To 2801 these cases she was called by the clergy of various denominations, in 33 cases by medical men, and in 91 cases by the sick persons or their friends, and in 28 cases by the Nuisance Inspector and others.—Mrs. Preston seconded the motion which was carried.—lt was decided that the balance in hand should he kept as a reserve fund or nuclues for the future conduct and extension of the work, and that an effort be made to raise the amount of sub- scriptions so as to cover the annual expenditure. On the propojtion;of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mrs. Lake. the retiring members of the Committee (Mrs. Wood, Mrs. Lightburn and Mrs. Meadowcroft) were re-elected.—Miss Taylor and Mrs. Edwin Imison were re-elected members

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
INSPECTION BY THE PROVISION TRADE.

A large party of gentlemen representing the provision trade in Manchester and Liverpool were on Wednesday -shown over a portion of the Ship Canal works by Mr. Henry Boddington, one of the directors of the company, and Mr. Marshall Stevens, the manager. They assem- bled at Pomona Docks at 10 a.m., and were conveyed from that point over the contractor's line to Barton, Irlam, Thelwall, Latchford, and Wilderspool. At the latter place they were entertained to luncheon at the Saracan's Head Hotel. After the luncheon Mr. Dowdall proposed, and Mr. J. D. Copeman seconded, a vote of thanks to the directors of the company.—Mr. Henry Bod dington, in replying to the vote, said he believed that Liverpool, their great opponents, were coming. ,to see that the canal might do them some good Mr. Marshall Stevens, having been called upon to say a few words about the traffic, said that in 1639 the total import of provisions was 20,000 tons. Compare that with 1889, and they had 715.000 tons of provisions brought into this country. They did not need to take anything from Liverpool, the simple increase of the imports was sufficient for them. On bacon they were going to save the traders Bs. per ton and on preserved meats 9s. per ton. (Hear, hear.) The party then walked to Acton Grange, where they inspected the deep cutting and deviation of the London and North-Western Rail- way, after which they returned to Salford by the con- tractor's train.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.

BY IN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. That the Committee appointed to consider upon the advisability of forming Widnes into a Corpora- tion town, have decided to recommend the Local Board to apply for a charter of incorporation, sub- ject to the approval of the ratepayers. That it is highly probable, in fact certain,the Board will adopt this recommendation, and the ratepayers unanimously approve. That steps will then at once be taken for the division of the town into wards. That it is proposed that there shall be six wards, each ward to be represented by three councillors and one alderman. That the governing body will thus be composed of 24 members instead of 15 as at present. That Runcorn Tonic Sol Fa Choir made a very good start for the season, on Monday evening, and, as it is an institution deserving of every support, it is to be hoped it will go on progressing until the desires of their able conductor, Mr. Halford are realised. That the night schools commenced by Runcorn School Board are proving even more successful than was anticipated by the advocates of more educational facilities for the town. That there are now -about 80 pupils for the various subjects, and Mr. Moulton and his assis will have a busy time of it.
tants 110'

- That the science and art classes are also likely to prove a success, and it is gratifying to learn that Mr. J. Knowles, of the Runcorn Alkali Works intend to open a class for the teaching of technico- logical chemistry, or in other words, alkali manu- facture, which being the principal trade, is a most important-subject for the young men of the town to team. That as regards the teaching of science. and technical instuction generally, Runcorn is very much behind many other towns, and Widnes in particular, where the Technical Education Act has been adopted and put in force. That at the next meeting of Runcorn School Board, Mr. Hewitt will move a resolution asking the Board of Commissioners to adopt the Technical I Education Act for Runcorn. That it is hoped the Board willipass the resolution and that the Commissioners will accede to the re- quest. That by the death of Mr. Ebenezer Timmins, Runcorn has lest a public man of most estimable character, and one whose name was known far and wide as a most skilful engineer in the line of busi- ness which he adopted. That Mr. Timmins was gifted with great fore- sight, and indomitable perseverance, qualities which enabled him to build up a successful business, and to become the largest individual employer of labour in the town. That Mr. Timmins has been in very poor health for several years past, but he never relinquished the oversight of his works, and he died in harness. That he can ill be spared. "lie wao a man, take him for all in all. We shall not look upon his like again."

div.head: OXFORD UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES
div.p: OXFORD UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES
AT RUNCORN. "WEALTH AND WAGES."

The first of a series of lectures on " Problems of wealth and industry," under the Oxford University Extension Scheme, was delivered in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Thursday evening, to a large audi- ence. The lecturer for the course is Mr. Ilurbert Llewellyn Smith, 8.A., B.Sc., and in introducing him to the audience, the Rev. Canon Wood, the chairman, dealt at some length with the subject of political economy. He said we were gradually ar- riving at the idea that the State ought not to be simply a field in which the strongest was to get to the front, although, perhaps, that was better than that the State should be a field in which the man who is born in the best position should always keep at the front. We were learning to understand that the State ought to be a con- dition of things in which each individual served the State in the best way he could, and in return was cared for by the State in such a way that his life and his powers should be developed as best they might be. Be- tween these two general ideas, one of giving the indivi- dual liberty to do the best he could for himself, and the other of treating man as a unit of a great mass, and that the mass ought to take care of the unit, and the unit'eught to give service to the mass —between these ideas there might be a great conflict. At any rate there was no doubt these were two dominating influences in this country and other countries in Europe at the present time. In conclusion Canon Wood explained that political economy was the science which taught them how things ought to be man- aged by the State.—The Lecturer said he wished to guard himself most especially at the beginning against any idea that he came there to teach them the whole of political economy. Neither six lectures nor sixty lec- tures would be enough to exhaust the subjects which came into their view when they began to trace out the •nerations of economic laws in one sphere and in another; .1 he could do was to suggest and to stimulate interest in the economic or social problems which surrounded them; and the best result he could hope for was that they might go away with the idea that there was a great deal more to be learned in political economy. In politi- cal economy the problems they were concerned in were the problems of every day life, and were of burning in- terest to men in their actual practical work. There was nothing more wonderful than the way in which every member of a civilized society was unconsciously bound to every other member. His actions affected directly or indirectly hundreds and even thousands besides himself. Everyone in a civilized state of society got more from society than he contributed it to, and he emphasised the importance of a study of the industrial mechanicism ef society. It was to the science that stud- ied this mechanism that they gave the name of political economy. Describing wealth, the lecturer said it was not the same as money. To measure a nation's wealth by its store of gold would be as vain as to expect a bundle of concert tickets to gratify a man's desire for music. Money was only part of a nation's weal,h so long as it was useful. There were two agents in the making of wealth—nature and man. Nature sup- plied the raw material and man converted it into wealth. Without material they could not have production, and man was utterly unable to increase or decrease, the amount of matter in the world. He was unable to create energy; he could only utilize it, and in addition of utility to matter was labour. Even the shopkeeper was a pro- ducer in so far as he added utility to the article lie sold by placing it in the hands of the consumer. It was from the land indirectly that came all the materials of which wealth was made. Man's contribution was his labour, which consisted of the power of moving matter in such a position as would make it capable of supply human wants. As to the reasons for making wealth, man, said the lecturer, worked because he wants; because he was was conscious of certain unsatisfied desires. He warned the audience that the most pressing problem for econo- mists to take up was the right direction of human wants. They must not believe that mere increase of wealth or that a more equitable distribution of wealth was a solu- tion of the problem. The problem to be solved was the proper direction of the consumption. (Apple use.) Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, (hon. secretary to the local com- mittee), announced that a class would be held at the close of each lecture, and the examination would be held at'the conclusion of the course if a sufficient number of candidates attended the classes.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

A RUNAWAY TRAIN. Part of a goods trains ran away down a decline on the Great Eastern Railway, near Shenfield, yesterday morning, and fell over an embankment. The guard was was severely hurt. THE. LONDON DOCK DISPUTES. The arrangement which the corn porters have finally accented, includes a halfpenny per quarter advance in one hold, and a penny in another. They are expected to resume work immediately. MR. GLADSTONE'S MEETINGS. Mr. Gladstone, who will arrive at Edinburgh on the 20th inst., will address meetings at the Corr: Exchange on the 21st, at West Calder on the 23rd, at Dalkeith on the 25th, at the Music Hall, Edinburgh, on the 27th, and at Dundee on the 29th. ILLNESS OF LADY ROSEBERY. Speaking at a luncheon given in his honour yesterday by the Corporation of Glasgow, Lord Rosehery said his wife was very ill, but she was facing it with strength and all the forces of a good constitution, and he hoped, under God's providence, that she would soon rec, ver.

div.head: MR: GLADSTONE AND TELE WEINLEY ACT.
div.p: MR: GLADSTONE AND TELE WEINLEY ACT.

.--.— Mr. Gladstone has sent a post-card to a Nottingham gentleman, bearing yesterday's date, as follows, concern- ing the M'Kinley Tariff Bill :—" Sir,—The kPliinley Act is, as you will suppose, in my eyes a deplorable error, at- tended with severe and cruel consequences to innocent persons. I shall certainly desire to find an opportunity of offering remarks upon it in Midlothian.—Very faith- fully and obediently yours, W. E. GLADSTONE." THE PREMIER'S CARRIAGE AND HIS COACHMAN.

The Marquis of Salisbury's carriage, which was being conveyed to London from Dieppe, was on Thursday de- I tained at Newhaven, the Customs authorities having found concealed in it about two and a half gallons of brandy and sweetened spirits, together with a number of cigars, the combined duty on which amounts to about £l4. The coachman who was accompanying the carriage was also detained. THE TRAGIC SEQUEL TO AN ELOPEMENT. At Bilston, yesterday afternoon, John Wise, aged thirty-seven, an ironworker, was committed for trial at the Assizes for the wilful murder of Mary Davies, a married woman, at Deepfields, in August last. Prisoner was enraged because his wife had run away with Mrs. Davies's son, a young fellow of eighteen, and believing the mother had kept him in the dark in the matter, he shot her with a revolver, causing her death, and then at- tempted to kill himself. TriE ECCLES ELECTION. MR. ROBY AND THE TEMPERANCE PARTY. Mr. Roby, the Liberal. candidate, yesterday morning was waited upon by a deputation from the Church of England Temperance Society, who asked him to support their bill for the giving direct veto to the people. Mr. Roby expressed himself in favour of giving the control of licenses to elected boards instead of magistrates, and declined to entertain the idea of compensation for publi- cans deprived of their licenses by such boards.

div.head: SLAVIN AND M'AULIFFE AGAIN.
div.p: SLAVIN AND M'AULIFFE AGAIN.

Yesterday, Slavin and M'Auliffe again appeared at Lambeth Police Court. Inspector Harvey gave evi- dence supporting that of Inspector Chisholm, as to the violence used in the fight at the Ormonde Club. Mr. Purcell, on behalf of Slavin, submitted that the Treasury had not made out that the blows given were unlawful. The magistrate said it appeared to him that the defend- ants fought fiercely, and with utter disregard of conse- quences. He intended committing them for trial. The defendants' counsel then tendered evidence.

div.head: TIPPERARY TRIALS.
div.p: THE TIPPERARY TRIALS.
DISAPPEARICE-OF-M-ESSRS. DILLON AND W. O'BRIEN. REPORTED FLIGHT TO AMERICA.

A special correspondent says :—I hear from a source which is likely to be well informed that Mr. Dillon and Mr. W. O'Brien sailed from Queenstown to America. Anyhow, they have not yet arrived in Tipperary for the resumption of their trial, and their friends admit that they are missing. If this should prove to be correct there will have to be a further and longer adjourn- ment. A later telegram says :—Roth gentlemen have left the country, though not by the route I stated in my last. Their bail, £l,OOO apiece, will of course, be forfeited, but the money will be paid by the organisation. There is great excitement in the town of Tipperary. WARRANTS ISSUED.

At the sitting Of the Court, on the of the twelve defendants being read over, there was no response in the case of Mr. W. O'Brien and Mr. Dillon. All the other defendants were in their places. The Bench, having asked if the absentees were legally represented, and a "reply having been received in the negative, Mr. Ronan asked that the usual order should be made respecting their recognisance. Mr. Healy asked that the bonds should be read. After some further remarks the court adjourned until twelve o'clock. On the court re-assemb- ling, Mr. Ronan applied to the court to append the usual certificate for non-appearance to the bail bonds of Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien. Mr. Healy submitted that the sure- ties had fulfilled their obligations when Messrs. O'Brien and Dillon appeared at court on the first day. After some further argument, Mr. Irwin, presiding magistrate, said the Bench were of opinion that although the charge had been amended it was still substantially the same as was originally formulated. They would therefme give the usual certificate of non-attendance, as prescribed by statute. Mr. Ronan then applied for an adjournment until next day, in order to enable the Crown to consider what steps they slaould take. The application was

DEATH OF MR. it H. KERR.

--- The death took place on Wednesday at his resi- dence. Spark Hall, Stretton, of Mr. Robert Hutchin- son Kerr. Deceased was the proprietor of the Dail= wireworks. .Warrington, and so late as Saturday last he was attending to matters of busi- ness at his office. On Sunday he attended divine worship at Stretton Church, but on Monday morn- ing as he was coming to Warrington he had a severe attack of illness. From this he never recovered, and died as stated on Wednesday. Mr. Kerr was a native of Scotland, having been born near Dumfries forty-five years ago, but he had been in Warrington a large number of years. He married a daughter of Mr. Smith, the proprietor of the Dallam iron- workers,and of these works he became sole proprietor about two years ago. Mr. Kerr did not take any prominent part in the public business of Warring- ton, but he displayed much interest in the parochial affairs of Stretton where he resided. He was a pronounced Conservative in politics. He leaves a family of four children, Mrs. Kerr having died at the beginning of this year. The funeral takes place to-day at Stretton Church.

div.head: LECTURE ON THE REV. FATHER M A.THE W.
div.p: LECTURE ON THE REV. FATHER M A.THE W.

The opening meeting of the new session in con- nection with Cairo-st. Sunday School Temperance Society was held on Monday evening, when the Rev. F. K. Freeston delivered a popular lecture on "Father Mathew." The meeting was held in the Schoolroom, Cairo-st. The chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Birchall, who, in opening the proceed- ings, remarked that of all the great, good, and useful men Ireland had produced, he doubted whether any one had done more real service to the country, or, perhaps to the world, than Theobald Mathew. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. F. K. Freeston then proceeoed with his lec- ture, which was divided into two parts—Part 1, " Patriot, preacher, and priest ; " part 2. "The Apostle of Temperance." The rev, gentleman remarked that he wished he could have lived in the time when all the en- • thusiasm which Father Mathew must have called forth was in the air. Few men, English, Scotch, or Irish, had been able to call forth the enthusiasm of other men more directly and more usefully than this Irish Catholic priest. His reasons for dealing with the subject were , these—First, because Father Mathew was a good man; second, because he was a great teetotaller: and third. because Warrington had not been without its part in the Father Mathew movement. It had held a meeting on his behalf. There was another reason, and that was that one of the earliest, truest, and longest friends of Father Mathew was, he rejoiced to think, a former minister (still living) of Cairo-street, Chapel. (Applause) What held his hearers spell-bound beneath the pulpit, and moved the inmost hearts of even those who had come to church to criticise him ?—for, like all public characters, he was open to criticism. The answer was this. Father Mathew was neither a theologian, a scholar, nor an orator; but he had the eloquence of earnestness, and the power of love. (Applause.) Utterly free from all sectarian pride—because from the beginning to the end of his work he never made his Catholicism weigh on either side—he worked for the work's sake. He kept aside his theology as well as his politics, and the result was that he won the respect of Protestant and Catholic alike. He was filled with a burning sym- pathy for the people. (Applause.)—On the motion of Mr. Hirchall, seconded by Mr. Jones, a vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Freeston.

GUNPOWDER SUPERSEDED. By a Gun firing from 50 up to 300 shots without recharging. The mechanism is simple in construction. There is an entire absence of flame, smoke and dirt, and itis practically noiseless. • There is no recoil, with perfect safety and great penetration and precision. The Gun is light, elegant and inexpensive. Any form of projectile can be used. There is a complete absence of emanations such as result from the use of gunpowder. The charge is not affected by water. After firing, the exhausted reservoir can be replaced in a few seconds. The reservoirs are practically indestructible. THE GIFFARD GUN & ORDNANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. LONDON Copthall House, Copthall Avenue, London, B.C. BIRMINGHAM Midland Buildings, New Street, Birmingham. PROSPECTUS. M. Paul Giffard—the inventor (with his brother), of the well-known Giffard Injector—has, after many years study and at great outlay, perfected his system for the use of liquefied gas as a substitute for gunpowder or other explo- sives, to the satisfaction of some of the leading authorities in Europe. Since perfecting the'6, 8 and 12 millimetre guns as applied to sporting and rifle purposes, and also pistols of varied calibre. M. Paul Giffard has been devoting his entire attention to the perfection of a rifle suitable for military pur- poses, as also the application of his invention to cannon and other warlike instruments, in which he claims to have already achieved results sufficiently satisfactory to justify his belief that the adaptation of liquefied gas for war materials will be successful. This Company is formed to acquire and work M. Giffard's Gun and Ordnance patents, together with all improvements thereupon, for the United Kingdom, India, and the whole of the British Colonies with the exception of Canada. The validity of the patent is upheld by Mr. T. Aston, Q.C., &c., and Mr. Roger W. Wallace, Barrister-at-Law, and by Mr. W. Lloyd Wise, President of the Institute of Patent Agents, &c. It is the intention of the Directors to dispose of the rights and royalties in India and the Colonies to subsidiary com- panies The Vendors have had many inquiries in this direc- tion, and they anticipate- that this Company will realise a large sum on the conclusion of these negotiations. The Veudors state that they have already entered into a contract for the sale of the rights for the United States of America, including Noel and South America excepting Canada, for a very large sum to the principal firm of gun and ammunition manufacturers in that country, and that they have received substantial offers from the leading manufacturers in the prin- cipal European countries to whom the guns have been sub- mitted, and whose approval has been accorded. The completion of the negotiations in regard to these is now pending. •The Chamber of Commerce of St. Etienne have signified their appreciation of this invention, by awarding to Monsieur Paul Giffard tke unusual distiuction of a gold medal and an award of 10,000 trances. During the past thirty-five years, Monsieur Paul Giffard has done much to estrich science by valuable discoveries which have been widely adopted to the advantage of the commercial community, and his•rank as a scientist is univers- ally acknowledged. In 1853, in conjunction with his brother Henry, Monsieur Paul Giffard invented the well-known Giffard Injector which is now very largely used in works using steam-power. From that period up to 1865, the energies of the two brothers were directed towards further scientific discoveries. Monsieur Paul Giffard is the original inventor of the cold air machine (or refrigerator) used for the preservation of fresh meat, &c., and in 1879 was the successful competitor with that inven- tion at the Academy of Science and Medicine, the Society of Health and at the Municipal Council of Paris, against thirty- two European and foreign competitors consisting of the most noted engineer 3. He is also the inventor of the piston bearing his name, together with various apparatus for the production of vacuum, and for the liquefaction of gases. Since the year 1872 the delivery of telegraphic letters in Paris has been effected with extraordinary rapidity by M. Paul Giffard's Pneumatic Tube System, which has now been applied throughout Paris. In 1871 he commenced his practic- al experiments at the works of the Paris Gas Cempany for the compression of steam and air, and the liquefaction of gases. The result has been the invention by M. Paul Giffard of his method for the production of liquefied gas, in a form which is under absolute control, as a substitute for gunpowder or other explosives. The liquefied-gas gun appears to be destined to create a new era in the manufacture and use of all classes of sporting guns and rifles, also pistols and saloon arms. By it many of the difficulties which hinder the adoption of magazine rifles are obviated. Guns of 6, Sand 12 millimetres are capable, ac- cording to their calibre, of firing from 50 to 300 Consecutive shots without recharging. The following are the claims advanced by M. Paul Giffard ,in respect of his new liquefied-gas Gun : • 1. Absence of the usual report, fire, smoke, dirt, and smell. 2. Great precision, the force used being capable of the most accurate adjustment. 3. No recoil. 4. No heating of the gun, even when fired with the greatest rapidity. 5. The gun is small, light, and inexpensive, and can be handled with perfect safety. 6. The projective power does not deteriorate, but is as effective after a lapse of twelve months as when the reservoir or cartridge is first loaded, and is not affected by damp. 7. The reservoir containing the liquefied gas is small and light, and the cost is very small. 8. Spherical or elongated zonical bullets and small shot can be used, The guns can be seen and tried at the Offices of the Com- pany on application to the secretary. In order to realise the practical advantages of this inven- tion, it is only necessary to remember that the gun is sup- plied with a metallic reservoir charged with liquefied gas, fixed under the gun, and holding, according to the calibre, from 50 to 300 charges. These may be discharged in rapid succession as may be desired, without loss of effect. To re- charge the weapon it is only necessary to substitute a full re- servoir for the empty one ; this can be instantly done, the Reservoirs being made interchangeable. They are light and cheap, practically indestructable, and can easily be supplied through gunsmillis. A In the introduction of an invention of this nature, applic- able as it may be to so many purposes other than the propul- sion of projectiles, it will be readily seen that it is almost im- possible to form an accurate estimate of profits. The owners of the patents are themselves so satisfied upon this point that they have covenanted with the Directors to take, at the option the latter, the whole or any part of their purchase consideration in fully paid shares of the Company, and the promoters have undertaken to pay the whole of the prelimi- nary expenses up to allotment. The purchase price of the Giffard patents, patent rights and improvements for the United Kingdom. India, and all the British Colonies, with the exception of Canada, including the whole of the expenses up to allotment and the guarantee- ing of the working capital, has been fixed by the Vendors at £200,000. The following Contract has been entered into, viz.— , A Contract, dated the 2nd day of October, 1890, and made between the Giffard Inventions Trust, Limited, of the first part, and the Giffard Gun and Ordnance Company, Limited, of the second part. During the negotiations for the purchase of the property and the formation of the Company, arrangements have been entered into in connection therewith, as to the payment of the preliminary expenses, the guaranteeing of the-necessary working capital. &c. Applicants for shares shall be deemed to have notice of such contracts and to have waived the specification of the names, the parties thereto, and the dates thereof whether under section 38 of the Companies' Act, 1867. or otherwise. Applications for Shares should be made on the forms accompanying the Prospectus, and forwarded, with the deposit of 2/6 per share, direct to the Bankers of the Company or by letter to the Secretary, stating the number of Shares required, and accompanied by a deposit of 2/6 per share. Wkere no allotment is made, the deposit will be returned to the applicant in full, and where the number of shares alloted is less than the number applied for, the surplus will be credited in reduction of the further amount payable on allotment. Copies of the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Company, and the above specified Contract, can be in- spected at the offices of the Solicitors to the Company. Prospectuses and Forms of Application for Shares can be obtained at the offices of the,Company, or from the Bankers. Brokers or Solicitors, LONDON, 2nd October, 1890.

Lee, Deputy-Chairman; W. H. Bailey, Henry Boddington. Jacob Bright, M.P., John K. Bythell, W. J. Crossley, Charles J. Galloway, Alexander Henderson, Sir Edward Jenkinson, K.C.8., Joseph Lee, S. R. Glyn, Mills, Currie. and Co., 67, Lom- bard-street. London; and the National Provincial Bank of England, Limited, 94, Mosley-street. Manchester. The Company was incorporated in 1885 by special Act of Parliament, 48 and 49 Victoria cap. 188, with a Share Capital of £8,000,000, and has power to borrow under that Act £1,812,000, and has exercised such power to the extent of £1,359,000. By the Company's Act of 1887, authority was given to divide the Share Capital into £4,000.000 Ordinary Shares and £4,000,003 Preference Shares. Of the Ordinary Shares. £3,750.000 have been allobted, and the Contractor is under agreement to take the remainder unissued on account of his contract in paid-up shares in lieu of cash if required by the Company. The whole of the Preference Shares have been allotted. 27 per Share have been celled up on the Ordinary and Preference Shares. By the Manchester Ship Canal (Various Powers) Act, 1893. the Company were authorised to borrow on morgage of their undertaking, in addition to the £1,81200 authorised by the said Act of 1885, and subject thereto, any sum or sums not exceeding in the whole £600,000, The Ship Canal with its docks and railways and their revenue, as well as the Bridgewater Canals and their revenue, will be the security for the borrowing powers authorised by the Company's Acts of 1885 and 1890. The cost of the whole undertaking will be upwards of £10,000,000. The Bridgewater Canals have been worked with success since they were acquired by the Company,the revenue derived there- from oeing more than sufficient to pay the interest on the whole of the borrowing powers under the Act of 1885. The Company has purchased for the purposes of the Ship Canal 4,100 acres of land at a cost of £986,497 which has already enhanced in ' value. The Directors hope to be able to open lower section of the Canal (Eastham to Weston Point) early in 1291, and the higher section by the time fixed by the contracts. 42, DEINSGITE, MANCHESTER, 9th October, 1890. REUBEN PEARSON, AFTER more than 25 years' experience in the treatment of disease, is pleased to be able to commend to the public the testimony, voluntarily offered by many of hie past patients. In cases of Rheumatism, Gout, Sciatica and Lumbago, his Massage and other treatmenthas proved marvellously success- ful. For some years past he has made this treatment a spe- cial feature and study, and in the cases he has had under the sanction and supervision of Medical men, he has produced re- sults which even they admit have been singular and excep- tional. " REUBEN'S HYDRO," 49, Lord Street, Leigh, Lancashire, July 12th. DEAR SIR, It is with gratitude and love that I am writing to such a I gentleman as you, Mr. Pearson, who has done so much for the benefit of my health. You will perhaps remember me coming to your establishment at Hale-road, in August. 1886, quite crippled in my hands and feet with the Rheumatic and Chalk Gout, and after staying for a few weeks with you. I returned home at the end of six weeks, and I have never felt anything of the Rheumatic or Gout since. I can both use my hands and can walk quite well. Thanks be to God for it, for I am sure if I had not come to you and received your treatment, I should never have been able to walk, but should have been a cripple for life ; I had been under two eminent doctors for several months before I came to you, but I kept failing and going worse. I shall ever feel thankful and grateful to you. My wife joins me in kind regards to you for restoring me to %ealth, and hoping by the help of God I may remain so. I am Dear Sir, yours, JAMES COLLIER, Builder and Contractor, Leigh. REUBEN'S HYDRO', ALTRINCHLM. EXTRA CHARGE AFTER 8 P.M.
